Remitting Phantom Grain Levies to Relieve the Burden of Indemnity
Originally this monastery held an estate at Wengyuan, donated by the Xie family of the local villagers.

It had been given to the Sixth Patriarch for the upkeep of incense and lamps, yielding a fixed annual revenue of one hundred and twenty taels of silver. In the sixth year of Wanli a certain Lin Huan, a wandering scholar and a friend of the prefectural vice-magistrate Wang, was lodged in this monastery. He coveted something from the monks and, failing to get it, slandered them to the vice-magistrate, saying that this estate brought in rich profits and that all of it went to the monks. The vice-magistrate believed him; and as he happened to be acting as prefect, he diverted sixty taels of the estate’s revenue to offset the phantom grain levy owed by the boat-dwelling households of Qujiang, and reported the arrangement to the two provincial commissions and the circuit offices, fixing it as a standing regulation. The sixty taels retained by the monastery were further depleted because the tenant farmers were cunning and obstinate and fell into arrears, so that the monks were endlessly implicated. They appealed to the higher authorities again and again, spending more than a thousand taels in the end, yet could not obtain exemption. Later Commander Liu proposed that the prefecture report in detail and that the surplus from the tax office at Hanhuang — drawn from the commander’s military pay allotment — be appropriated to make up the difference, so as to spare the monks this burden; and for a long time this arrangement stood unchanged. But in the gengzi year of Wanli the tax commissioners were sent out, and the tax office revenue was taken into the inner eunuch establishment. The monks accordingly appealed to Commander Dai, who graciously permitted matters to proceed as before. Afterwards, however, the tax commissioner sent his own officers to collect the levy, leaving no surplus to appropriate. When the Master learned of this he went in person to the commander’s office to state the case, and received an order to the county to find some unobstructed source of compensation and not to burden the monks further. The county searched repeatedly and found nothing; so it was proposed to levy a tax on the small boats carrying grain on the streams and rivers that run through the hills, which yielded twenty-six taels — not yet enough. A further search revealed that opposite the hills at Mengli there was an old ‘poison-field’ that had never been assessed. Its rent was set at thirty-four taels, making up the full sum; the proposal was reported and approved. From that time the evil was permanently sealed off from the monastery gate — all through the protective power of the Supreme Commander. Once this burden was lifted, however, the tenants of the estate remained cunning and obstinate, and because they lived across the county border they were hard to control; through this land they brought ceaseless trouble upon the monks. Assessing the cost of pursuing the land, the community deliberated and decided to sell the estate and use the proceeds to redeem nearby fields belonging to the monastery. They petitioned the commander, who referred the matter to the circuit, which ordered the prefecture and county to deliberate; and it was judged expedient. But the tenants, who had farmed the land for generations and regarded it as their own, refused to let it be sold to others and were willing to resurvey and increase the rent, vowing to hold the monastery’s property in trust forever without substitution. Commissioner Xu, the second assistant magistrate of Qujiang, who was acting in Wengyuan, assembled the tenants and had the land measured; the fields proved indeed to be in excess, and so beyond the regular rent an additional fourteen-odd taels were assessed, reported to the higher authorities, and approved in detail. The tenants were then bound to pay into the treasury each year on an agreed date. At that time the abbot and monks of the monastery agreed that, as the additional rent had come about through the Master’s efforts, it should revert to the Master as the restored permanent endowment; and so it was joined with the incense-and-lamp revenues of the Wujin Hermitage and given over to the Chan hall for the support of the community, to stand forever as a fixed rule. This one matter was indeed an endless scourge at the monastery gate. Earlier it was Commander Liu who by expedient measures held it in check; in the end it was Lord Dai who cut the burden off forever and turned it into a blessing for later times. Thus we know that the Dharma is entrusted to kings and ministers: without the great strength of outer protection, how could it be preserved forever? The full case files are kept in the prefecture and county offices.
Recovering the Patriarch’s Mountain to Bar Encroachment

The patriarchal mountain of Caoxi is shaped like an elephant, its head and tail, front and rear, clearly distinguished; the whole range behind the monastery forms its body. The Zisun estate there was one of the twelve flower-and-fruit gardens visited by the Patriarch in his lifetime. Long ago seven monks dwelt there under the name Little Nanhua, and so it had been for ages. In the first year of Chenghua, Shaozhou first opened up fields and fixed their boundaries, and the whole of this mountain was swallowed up by the powerful. At that time the monk Mancang of Shenggong submitted a memorial to the court, which ordered the governor and censor to survey and restore the monastery’s property, beginning with the punishment of those who had occupied the Zisun estate. Later, because the monks grew numerous and undisciplined, the nearby residents nibbled away at the land until it could no longer be held, and the monks returned to the monastery, abandoning the estate. In the twentieth year of Wanli the bully Jiang Yingdong, under the pretense of buying monk-owned fields, seized the whole range behind the mountain for the sake of geomancy, so that the elephant’s spine was cut in two from the patriarchal mountain, and felling gradually encroached upon the inner lands. The Master was grieved and said: ‘From this time on the patriarchal mountain will pass wholly into private hands.’ He therefore roused and urged the monks to appeal to the commander’s office, which referred the matter to the circuit; the prefect was ordered to inspect in person, and the acting magistrate of Zhaoqing, Subprefect Wan, went up the mountain, surveyed the ground, and set boundary stones, ruling that the former fields be redeemed by the monks to cut off the source of calamity. The Master himself raised two hundred taels of silver and redeemed the fields, so that together with the woodlands of the rear mountain they became the perpetual endowment of the Chan hall — thus not only preserving the patriarchal mountain but securing an everlasting possession for the hall. Yet for this the Master incurred resentment, and lawless monks colluded with outsiders to do him harm; in the end, however, a firm stone tablet was set up, a veritable diamond banner.
Opening the Chan Hall to Secure the Root

One day the Master addressed the assembly: ‘A monastery’s Chan hall is like a state’s school — a place for nurturing vessels of talent. From ancient times those who governed a state took the storing of talent as the root, and so it is with the Dharma gate. From the time Bodhidharma came from the West, the robe and bowl stopped at Caoxi. Under the Sixth Patriarch more than thirty men awakened to the Way, and of them Nanyue and Qingyuan were the foremost. The Baolin Chan hall was the birthplace of the patriarchs; hence of the more than seventeen hundred men recorded in the lamp transmission of Chan halls throughout the realm, all came from the single line of Caoxi — like the Zhu and Si rivers of Confucius’s school. Thus this mountain’s Chan hall is the root ground of the Chan school. Yet as the years passed and the monks failed in their charge, the Chan hall all but sank into oblivion. On its old site there were seven monks’ quarters jumbled together, two kitchens, and nine each of privies and pigsties, so that a pure and precious ground had become a dung heap.’ The Master grieved deeply over this. Reflecting that a monastery of a hundred years must be planted with people, he selected novices and trained them to maturity; for to teach without nurturing is like a farmer who knows how to sow but not how to weed, and can never reap a harvest. Without a Chan hall, on what would later generations rely? Day and night he pondered this, his heart scorched with anxiety. Surveying everywhere for suitable ground, he used his own robe-and-bowl funds and his own reduced rations to accumulate several tens of taels of silver, bought up vacant land, moved the monks’ quarters one by one, subsidizing the cost of building anew elsewhere, and exchanged the cleared ground for the Chan hall, measuring inch by inch and trading ten for one until at last the plot was even and square. Exhausting mind and strength, he raised a single compound for the Chan hall. Though it did not fully match the old plan, its scale was the utmost he could achieve. He further reflected that if it followed the common conventions of other places it could never last; so he established a ten-direction hall outside the mountain gate to receive wayfarers, while the inner hall housed only monks of this monastery, training younger students who devoted themselves to pure practice. Happily a fixed rule was formed, and the monks in the hall were numerous and impressive — a true practice ground. Since the Chan hall was now built, providing for so many mouths was difficult; so he assigned to it the thirty-one taels of rent from the hermitage that had supported the monastery’s restoration, and the fourteen taels of new rent from Wengyuan, together with the land and woodlands of the Zisun estate redeemed at their original price of over two hundred taels, and a tract of firewood mountain at Huangshan bought for a certain sum; and he exchanged a sandalwood-grove house of his own purchase for two monks’ quarters behind the kitchen. All was given over to the Chan hall as the enduring endowment of the restoration, to meet the costs of building and repair. This single establishment came to no less than a thousand taels, all borne by the Master alone. From then on the monks had enough food and clothing and propriety and righteousness flourished; so what the monks in the hall enjoy today is all the bitter toil and bloody sweat of the Master in those days. Can those who later live at ease not know its source? If the monks, having enough to eat, can also fill themselves with the food of Dharma, then the wisdom-life of the buddhas and patriarchs may rely on this to stand firm forever.
Appendix: The Unfinished Affinity

What is listed above follows the plan of the ten chapters of the Caoxi Gazetteer that the Master compiled; so I have gathered the main outlines of these matters and likewise divided them into ten sections, to show a single hair of the whole body. As for the finer details of practice that lie beyond thought and speech, they cannot easily be counted one by one. During those eight years of unremitting toil, his spirit was utterly spent: of what was accomplished, seven tenths was the work of clearing and opening, three tenths the work of building. The great Buddha hall was the one unfinished task — the Sixth Patriarch’s own unfinished task. He had long wished to undertake it, but his strength fell short. In the third month of spring in the wu-shen year, Lord Feng Wensuo, circuit inspector of Lingxi, came into the mountains to visit the Master and lodged in the hermitage. At night he dreamed of the Bodhisattva Guanyin appearing in a tall and mighty body, of dignified and majestic marks. Lord Feng bowed in reverence and praised that splendid adornment, and heard the Bodhisattva say: ‘That which is not adornment is called adornment.’ He had an awakening. Waking, he was overjoyed. At dawn he entered the hall to worship the Buddha and pay respects to the Bodhisattva, and saw that the rear pillars of the great hall were rotted and about to collapse, and that the three great Bodhisattva images were in grave danger. He pointed and said to the Master: ‘Why not repair this?’ The Master said: ‘I have long cherished this wish, but my strength has not been equal to it.’ Lord Feng asked: ‘What would it require?’ The Master said: ‘I would not dare undertake it for less than three thousand taels of silver.’ Lord Feng said: ‘I beg to take it upon myself with all my strength.’ The Master said: ‘If the benefactor truly rouses the great mind, it lies in a cough and a snap of the fingers.’ Lord Feng said: ‘It surely cannot be done by one man’s strength; let us plan it slowly.’ Returning, he saw Lord Dai, Grand Minister of War and Supreme Commander, and told him the reason. Lord Dai said: ‘When a child is about to fall into a well, the benevolent man crawls to save him; how much more when a great hall is about to topple and the holy images are in peril? This the humane heart cannot bear.’ He then spoke to Lord Feng and asked the Master to confer with him face to face. The Master was glad to hear it, and brought plans and specifications to visit Lord Dai. Privately reckoning from the plans, Lord Dai said: ‘What you propose is not yet enough.’ The Master said: ‘Buddha work is like a cloud in the sky; let this merely serve as the originating condition.’ Lord Dai at once vowed to undertake it. The Master said: ‘Matters of the Dharma gate cannot be bound by worldly rules, nor can they be expected to succeed quickly. If Your Excellency’s kindness bears it alone, I fear there may be inconvenience; the hearts of the many must be joined as one. It is enough if you lend the power of the Dharma to lead them.’ So ten circulars were drafted and sent to the provincial commissions, circuits, and prefectures, each to contribute. Before many days the commander, the two commissions, the circuit, and the prefecture had each donated a thousand taels. The Master went in person to western Yue to seek great timbers, shouldering every task himself. In the fourth month of the next year, jiyou, the timber was all transported to Mengli. The Master returned to the mountain, gathered the community, chose an auspicious day, and began work. Because obstructive monks’ quarters had first to be moved to vacant ground so that the dismantled materials could be piled there, one or two unruly monks, finding it inconvenient, incited the crowd to clamor like rebels. The Master let the matter rest for three days, sitting silently in the hermitage reading the Diamond Sutra, and then said: ‘This is precisely the fault of my own attachment to appearances.’ He thereupon composed the Diamond Cutter’s Resolution of Doubts, completing it in three days. The crowd then quieted. The instigator grew frightened, and, at a loss, falsely accused the Master of embezzling several hundred taels of the monastery’s money and of demolishing several halls. He laid the charges before the circuit and prefecture. When the Master heard it he said: ‘Any insult can be borne in patience; but to say that I have dipped my fingers into the permanent endowment’s money touches the great Dharma — how can I remain silent?’ He therefore produced the monastery’s pre-existing pure rules, the ledgers of receipts and expenditures, the warrants and receipts, and the names of the monks who had handled the funds, and reported all in full to the circuit, which referred it to the prefecture. Those who had handled the accounts over the years were summoned and audited; the Master was not implicated in the slightest. The abbot Yuanzu was convicted of embezzlement in his stead. The monks appealed again to the censor, who referred the case to the judicial office; the Master went in person to the hearing. In the fifth month of that year he drifted quietly out of the mountain and never entered the monastery again. Because there was no one to replace him as incumbent of the direct-pointing transmission, the Master, bearing the Dharma, did not leave his boat; he lived there two years. The boat broke, and he dwelt in a rented house for a year, enduring hardship, humiliation, illness, and distress of every kind. In the autumn of xinhai, Censor Wang toured the circuit, and the judicial administrator Jiang, mishearing the case, ruled that the Chan hall the Master had built and the endowments of mountain land and fields he had provided should all be adjudged to the Buddha hall in name, though in fact to the litigants, and further convicted the Master of lawlessness and deported him beyond the borders, while those who had labored before were all convicted as well. When the case went up, the censor wrote in his rescript: ‘Yuanzu stole and sold the monastery’s foundation, yet still plays the rogue: he is the great criminal against the Patriarch. So-and-so has done great service to the Sixth Patriarch; the lawbreaking monks are not sent away, while the meritorious are convicted instead, and even his Wujin Hermitage is seized. Is this to be regarded as the Dharma gate of equality?’ He then ordered Circuit Chief Liu to re-examine the matter thoroughly, and Subprefect Chen was again sent to the monastery. Going through the records one by one, every charge proved false. Yuanzu, in terror, died of himself; the case was closed by law. The incense and lamps of the Chan hall were placed under the Master’s disciple Yuanxiu, and thus the Sixth Patriarch’s threadlike line was preserved, and the Master’s heart and traces at last stood clear before the world. Those in authority urged him again and again to return to the mountain and finish his former work. The Master said: ‘A monk advances or withdraws according to conditions; now the conditions are exhausted.’ He declined on the plea of illness and went his way, vast and unconstrained. The Master then composed the Record of the Incense and Lamps of the Restored Caoxi Baolin Chan Hall, setting out the whole affair and having it carved in imperishable stone. It was the ninth month of autumn in the xinhai year of Wanli. His disciples earnestly begged him to stay, and he dwelt at Changchun Hermitage in Wuyang. The following year, guichou, illness made him restless, and he took up his staff for Nanyue. In the summer of bingchen he traveled east through Wu and Yue, mourning at the shrines of Master Zibai and Master Yunqi. Lord Wang Jingfeng of Huangmei, a Minister of War, wrote to Lord Chen Chishi of Fuliang, a Grand Counselor, to act as benefactor and keep the Master in retirement at Mount Kuang. In the summer of the following year, dingyi, the Master returned to Mount Kuang and built a hut below Wuru Peak. After the Master left Caoxi, the disciples he had taught were like infants bereft of a loving mother; day and night they thought of him, and to get him back was beyond hope. Four years later, in gengshen, Lord Wu, a provincial administrator, entered the mountain, saw the scale of the monastery, and sighed over it three times. The monks then told in full of the Master’s merit and virtue and of the longing in the hearts of all on the mountain. Lord Wu was filled with joy, vowed to be a protector of the Sixth Patriarch, and wrote to invite the Master back. Before long Lord Zhu, protector of the restoration, also arrived and with all his strength urged the Master to turn the Dharma wheel. From this one knew all the more that the Sixth Patriarch’s spirit is responsive and that the opportunity for the Dharma’s transformation in Lingnan still stands. This was the Master’s last chapter of affinity, and so I record it to show those who come after. Wang Anshun said: ‘How hard it is to establish merit and accomplish affairs — and not only in the undertakings of a dynasty; so too in the Dharma gate. Caoxi is the Zhu and Si of the Chan school; the monasteries of the realm and the patriarchs of the lamp transmission all come from one line — is this a small matter? Now a thousand years have passed, and its ruin and decay have reached this extreme; even were the Sixth Patriarch to appear again, he would find it hard. How fortunate that, borrowing the favor and spiritual power of the sage Son of Heaven, the Master came through adverse conditions and by his single strength renewed it, so that in less than eight years the work was more than half done. Not to speak of his two gifts of wealth and Dharma — his unshakable resolve, his willingness to taste hardship, slander, and humiliation as if they were honey, would be hard to find even among the ancients. As for the Master’s true compassion in dealing with beings and responding to conditions, he constantly said that one should be either a loyal minister of a worldly lord or a filial son of a loving father. Whenever he saw men bearing halberds in the ranks, great generals at the gate of the command, soldiers in files like geese, bowing their heads below the steps — their coming and going like sitting on a lotus and worshipping the golden immortals — he never once saw a sluggard’s face among them. And when the region was troubled and those in authority wrung their hands while the people trembled and could not rest their heads on their pillows, the Master silently wielded the power of compassion, resolving difficulties and dissolving quarrels, working unseen and in secret, turning the wheel among them, never once seeking to be known. If ever his integrity offended the times, so that every one of his disciples feared for him, the Master remained calm and bore no grudge at all. Not to speak of his wondrous awakening and profound subtlety, his lofty talents and unconstrained spirit — even in following conditions and responding to things he was of one plain and even mind. All who gathered would say with one voice: “Is this not what is called manifesting a responsive transformation body and teaching the Dharma according to kind? Otherwise, why do we venture to say that Lingnan’s Sixth Patriarch is the source of the Buddhadharma, and that we are fortunate a thousand years later to see him once again? Was he not long ago granted a prediction?” The Master’s mind is like empty space and cannot be measured; I have roughly recorded the outline of his deeds thus. The Master spent eighteen years in the ranks. His writings include the Caoxi Gazetteer, Notes on the Laṅkāvatāra, Comprehensive Exposition of the Śūraṅgama, The Lotus Blossom Marked Out, Sectional Exposition, The Diamond Cutter’s Resolution of Doubts, An Exposition of the Daodejing, On the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, An Exposition of the Hundred Dharmas and the Rules of the Consciousness-Only School, The Awakening of Faith and Sengzhao’s Treatises, An Exposition of the Inner Chapters of Zhuangzi, and The Great Learning’s Resolution of Doubts. His poetry is the Dream-Journey Collection, beginning from the time of his ordeal, together with Dharma talks and verses given to disciples — millions of words in all. Yet all were written amid his travels: whenever something was asked of him, he wrote as his mind prompted, never once sitting at ease to think it over. As for his brushwork, a scrap of paper from his hand was treasured by the world. Roughly viewed, what of the Master can be seen is but the leftover; what cannot be seen — how could it be reached by thought or speech? Someone asked: ‘Is he not what is called one who blends his light with the dust, subtle and darkly penetrating, so deep as to be unknowable?’ I said: ‘That too is but a forced description. If you would know my Master, please await one who is like my Master.’
