Record of the Restoration of Caoxi, Part Two
An Exhortation to Abstain from Wine, Addressed to the Attendant Lingtong (with Preface)

When I first came to Caoxi I carried a petal of incense and reverently paid my respects to the Sixth Patriarch. I saw the monk in charge of the stupa offering wine, at the new and full moons each month, to the attendant Lingtong. I asked the reason. The monk said: ‘The attendant was a man of Persia in the Western Regions. He came by sea to Guangzhou, heard of the Sixth Patriarch, and rejoicing, took refuge and vowed to serve as attendant, forever acting as Dharma protector and guarding the Caoxi practice ground. But his nature craved wine and he could not keep from drinking, and the Sixth Patriarch permitted him to drink in secret. This was wrongly handed down, and the ignorant, not understanding, made it a regular practice, which by habit has continued to this day, nearly a thousand years, with no one able to wash away the attendant’s stain.’ I, a disciple of the Dharma-ending age, having received the Patriarch’s embracing care, came to set Caoxi in order, and a full year has now passed. On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the xinchou year of Wanli — the day of our Buddha’s awakening — I conferred the precepts universally upon the assembled monks of the whole mountain. Fearing that foolish monks might cling to their delusion and not be transformed, I have cleared the attendant’s name with a single heart, to silence all mouths. Reverently taking up a petal of incense, I announced the Patriarch’s command and addressed the attendant: ‘Reverently I think of you, Lingtong: ask not whence you came; since you serve as Dharma protector, you should accord with utmost impartiality. In the beginning, when you heard the Patriarch teach, you heard that fundamentally there is not a thing; how did you fail to understand? Since you understood that fundamentally there is nothing, what five aggregates remain? How could one who has truly grasped emptiness take pleasure in wine? The Patriarch taught men to drink the nectar of dew, not to pour this dregs-water down a withered gut. I observe that the attendant never left the Patriarch’s side, hearing the Dharma all day long; how could he not know? Knowing truly and awakening long since, would he be deluded again and air his own family’s shame? I know the attendant has surely no such feeling. It is the foolish monks who do not understand and take it for truth, so that all are muddled and drunk day and night. Is the Patriarch not thereby burdened? I forbid the monks to drink wine; the monks use the attendant as their pretext. When monks break the Dharma, the attendant is made the ringleader. If this is not stopped today, delusion will spread from one to another. Alas, in this Dharma-ending age the monasteries wither; I pray the attendant to take thought for this betimes. If you would truly protect the Dharma, begin here. If the attendant does not drink, who will dare open his lips? I now bow my head and cry out in sorrow to the Patriarch: overturn the whole matter from the bottom, shatter this folly, break the mass of doubt, crush the drinking vessels, so that all alike realize the unborn and together ascend to buddhahood. Henceforth let the offerings be of the three virtues and six flavors, and let the attendant receive and enjoy them no differently from the Patriarch. Protecting the Dharma thus, his merit will be matchless; within and without all is pure, and the dust is swept away at once. The spiritual source gushes forth, the withered tree returns to spring, and mountains, rivers, and the great earth all turn the Dharma wheel together. Respectfully proclaimed.’
On the Origin of the Earth-Veins and Configuration of the Caoxi Patriarchal Ground
Spoken by Hanshan Deqing, the Recluse of Mount Kuang

The practice ground of the Caoxi patriarchal seat began with Tripiṭaka Master Zhiyao of Liang, who came from the Western Heavens to Wuyang and entered China. As his boat passed the mouth of the stream he scooped up water and drank it, and found it fragrant and sweet. He said: ‘This is water from the Western Heavens. Above its source there must be a holy place.’ So he followed the stream up and saw Elephant Mountain, and sighed: ‘This is exactly Mount Baolin of the Western Heavens.’ He then said to the villager Cao Shuliang: ‘This mountain is a holy practice ground. One hundred and seventy years from now a sage will appear here and teach the Dharma, saving countless beings. You should build a monastery and wait for him.’ Shuliang told the local magistrate, who memorialized Emperor Wu, and by imperial decree Baolin Monastery was built. This was the founding of the mountain. In the Yuanzhao period of Tang the Sixth Patriarch rose in Xinzhou, received the robe and bowl of Huangmei, and returned to Baolin. The monastery was then in ruins, and there remained only one nun named Wujin, a woman of the prefecture, living in a hermitage behind it. The Sixth Patriarch visited her. She was reading the Nirvāṇa Sutra, and he asked her about the words. The Patriarch said: ‘The words I do not recognize; you should ask me about the meaning.’ The nun said: ‘You do not even know the words — how can you know the meaning?’ The Patriarch said: ‘The wondrous meaning of all buddhas does not depend on letters.’ He then expounded it with all his strength. The nun knew he was no ordinary man and told her father, brothers, and neighbors, who led the crowd to rebuild the monastery and begged the Patriarch to dwell there. After nine months evil men came seeking him, and the Patriarch, mindful of Huangmei’s charge, fled and hid among the hunters between Huai and Hui for fifteen years. In the Yifeng period, at Faxing Monastery in Guangzhou, hearing two monks argue about wind and banner, the Patriarch said: ‘It is neither wind nor banner; it is the reverend gentlemen’s minds that move.’ The crowd was astonished and questioned him, and learned where the robe and bowl of Huangmei were. They asked him to teach the assembly, and he was shaved under the bodhi tree and escorted back to Baolin in Caoxi. From the bingwu year of Tianjian of Liang to the bingzi year, the first of Yifeng of Emperor Gaozong of Tang, one hundred and seventy years had passed, fulfilling the words of Tripiṭaka Master Zhiyao. The Patriarch taught the Dharma here for more than thirty years, and forty-three men under his seat awakened to the Way, with Nanyue and Qingyuan foremost. Thus the Way divided into two branches, and later five houses arose. So the single line of Chan recorded in the lamp transmission issued from Caoxi, like the Zhu and Si rivers of Confucius’s school. In the Patriarch’s later years those who returned to him grew daily more numerous, and the halls were cramped and narrow. He therefore visited the villager Chen Yaxian and said: ‘Old monk that I am, I would beg from you, benefactor, a patch of ground the size of my sitting mat. May I have it?’ Yaxian asked: ‘How wide is the monk’s sitting mat?’ The Patriarch showed it to him, and Yaxian agreed. The Patriarch spread the mat, and it covered the whole of Caoxi’s four boundaries, while the Four Heavenly Kings appeared and seated themselves at the four corners. Yaxian said: ‘I know the monk’s Dharma power is vast; but my great-great-grandfather’s grave is here. When you build in days to come, I beg that it be preserved; all the rest I gladly give up forever as a precious monastery.’ But this land is the descending vein of the living dragon and white elephant; it may be leveled at the sky but not at the ground. So he gave it, and it became a great Dharma assembly. This was the completion of the monastery. I have always reflected that the Chan gate’s Dharma way is desolate, and that the single line of the Chan school under heaven issues from Caoxi; now that its Way is not made manifest, the source must be choked, and it ought to be dredged. This has long been my vow. In the bingshen year of Wanli, for spreading the Dharma I met with calamity and was sent by imperial grace to Leiyang, and first paid my respects.

I paid my respects to the Sixth Patriarch and entered Caoxi, and observed the configuration of its mountains and rivers: it resembles an elephant crouching on the ground, tusks and feet clearly formed. Originally Baolin Monastery was enclosed within the left jaw, and the Patriarch’s hall sits exactly on the elephant’s trunk. Examining it closely, I saw that a road had been cut through the middle of the trunk, severing it in two. And I reflected that the elephant’s life lies in its trunk, which must have several joints; I saw that behind the Patriarch’s hall the ground was low and hollow, exposed to the full blast of the north wind, and sighed: ‘The mountain vein is already severed; this is why the Dharma way has withered.’ At that time the monks of the monastery were overrun by roving ruffians who plied slaughtering and wine-selling, and the practice ground could scarcely be preserved. So by various expedients I sheltered and set it in order. In the gengzi year Lord Zhu of this circuit, moved by deep compassion, repeatedly asked me to put it in order. When I first entered the mountain I blocked the road that came through the dragon vein, carried earth to build up a mound behind the Patriarch’s hall, dredged the Zhuoxi spring and led it into the kitchen, so that it circled before the hall and the community could drink from it; and I asked the supreme commander to order the county to drive out all the ruffians. Thus the practice ground was once cleansed: this was the first step of the restoration. I saw that the monastery’s old layout was jumbled and uneven and quite unseemly, hard to plan, and that the work was vast and could not be set right at once, with halls and monks’ quarters so blocked as to be impassable. Day and night I examined and pondered it, and at last divided the grounds according to the lie of the land into three sections, with the patriarchal seat as the central main shrine. First I opened up the cloisters, gateways, and spirit paths, to broaden its chest and open its true features. The left section is the ancient Baolin Monastery, with the abbot’s quarters as its center; below the front Dharma hall, where the patriarchs of old awakened to the Way, the Chan hall and the kitchen were all made into monks’ dwellings. I bought vacant land and moved eight monks’ quarters, and so recovered the old site, and built halls to house and train the community. The monks of this monastery had already been struggling for eight years; the cost had been enormous and my strength of mind was spent, and still my vow was unfulfilled. The great Buddha hall occupies the right section. I saw that the hollow before the hall was not yet filled level, that the Arhat Tower directly before the hall was sunken more than ten feet, that before the tower the tiger-sand blocked the chest, and that it was still wild mountain, with a single path issuing from the mountain gate, narrow as a carriage box and utterly without dignity. Pondering deeply why this was so, I realized that it was the Sixth Patriarch’s unfinished work from his later years. The foundation of the main hall was originally a pool, and examining the shape of the mountain, it was first the place where the elephant’s two tusks meet, where the water of the whole mountain gathered and pooled, and therefore it was the most numinous, with a dragon dwelling there; it was called Dragon Pool. The right jaw at the trunk was the lower sand before Yaxian’s ancestral grave, and is now the right arm of the Patriarch’s hall. I think that when the Sixth Patriarch begged the land from Chen Yaxian he wished to build a hall, and so first subdued the dragon, cut through the meeting place to form a channel, and let the water out; only then did he fill the pool to build the great hall. The hall was barely completed when the Patriarch entered nirvāṇa, and so the pool before the hall was never filled level, and the water channel was never put in order. Later men, taking advantage of this defect, built a tower over it, and below it fashioned images of the Heavenly Kings. Its carelessness and narrow meanness utterly destroy the general design. Thus the mountain vein is cut and the ground has lost its form; and so for a thousand years, searching the lamp transmission carefully, one sees not a single man emerge from Caoxi. From this we see: is the vein of the Way not bound to the vein of the earth? This is why day and night my heart is gnawed, and I cannot forget my attachment to this. So I first put the two sections roughly in order, with some sequence to them, and would next set the right section in order; its labor would be no less than when the Sixth Patriarch first founded the place. For from behind the mountain gate there are eight halls, all decayed; without relying on the power of divine transport, how could it be done? Earlier, in the wu-shen year, Lord Feng Wensuo of the Lingxi circuit entered the mountain and saw that the main hall was about to collapse, and roused his mind to rebuild it. He told Lord Dai, the supreme commander, who gladly pledged his aid, and for a time the commissions, circuits, prefectures, and counties all gave a thousand taels. Timber was procured first, and I managed it myself; but just as the wood was being brought to the mountain, demonic influence broke out and blocked the work. I then went my way vast and unconstrained. Now ten years have passed, and my body has grown frail while my vow is unfulfilled; it will become a case for a future life. But I reflect that the Buddhadharma and the Chan way, since Bodhidharma came from the West and the robe and bowl stopped at Caoxi, its vein and source, the wisdom-life of buddhas and patriarchs, and the upright qi of heaven and earth — all are like the Zhu and Si, bound up for all ages with the hearts of men and the ways of the world. It is the first and highest work of merit in our land of China. Though the Dharma has its rise and fall and the world its successions, the single vein of the great Way endures unchanging and imperishable through the exhaustion of kalpas, for it depends on the teaching of images and the numen of mountains and rivers. Beyond this, what other Dharma could serve as the constant order of heaven and earth? This is what I, in my folly, think of in repaying the Buddha’s grace and the sovereign’s grace, and dare not forget for a single breath. My original vow was to complete on the Sixth Patriarch’s behalf his unfinished work. The first is to rebuild the main hall, to make whole the dragon vein, to rebuild the channel cut before the hall as it was, and to leave a pool within to gather the water of the whole mountain and concentrate its numen. The Arhat Tower should be changed into the great Vairocana Hall as the main shrine; the tiger-sand before the tower should be taken and used to open a broad bright hall, with two cloisters built to house the arhats, and a Heavenly King Hall set before it to complete the main section. The outer mountain gate should follow the old plan. The bell and drum towers, which belong to the ancient Baolin Monastery and now stand in the left section before the Chan hall, cannot be moved; but outside the mountain gate two high terraces should be built on left and right, with bell and drum set upon them, to complete the monastery’s full design. As for the rest — the great Buddha behind the hall and the various storehouses — all should be renewed according to their old plan; the Dharma hall should be rebuilt, only setting its orientation right. With this one plan the three sections are gathered into a single monastery, and the work would be no less than at the first founding. I reflect earnestly that I am now old, my days are few, and what times are these? How dare I let such a thought spring up again? Yet judging by the great cycles of heaven and earth, I have lately seen that the Yellow River has run clear, that a sage has appeared again, that the Yao and Shun of the age have come forth, that ministers like Kui and Long have arisen; the transformation of the Three and the Five is at hand today. Leaning on the nurturing shelter of the sage and enlightened, the favor of the altars of state, and the meeting of wind and cloud, will there not be bodhisattvas of great mind who manifest responsive transformation bodies and perform great Buddha work? Alas, I am old; even if I fill a ditch, I leave this behind especially, to see the plan of building again, and wait for the true man destined for the age. Should there be one who undertakes it, let him follow this plan and pattern, and he will not betray my humble original vow, and will make whole the vein of the mountains and rivers. That will be the Sixth Patriarch appearing in the world again. Beneath the nine springs, this is my earnest hope.
The Master’s Dharma Words to the Monks of Caoxi

The Buddha said that a Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is like the udumbara flower — a flower that has not been seen, is not seen, and will not be seen; he spoke thus to express how exceedingly rare it is. Hence the ancients often said that to meet a good teacher is like seeing the udumbara flower open. A good teacher can be met for a moment only, and even that is not to be had — how much more to attend upon one day and night, following and conforming to him? Long ago, at the Lotus assembly, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, long since entered nirvāṇa, sat in his jeweled stūpa with his whole body undispersed, as though in meditation. At that time the attendants of all the buddhas of the ten directions, and the whole assembly on Vulture Peak, wished to see Prabhūtaratna and could not. Only by the Tathāgata’s spiritual power were the doors of the jeweled stūpa opened, and suddenly a million gods and men beheld him at one time, and each who saw him obtained the acceptance of the unborn Dharma, while those who roused the mind of unsurpassed bodhi were beyond counting. Now consider the Sixth Patriarch: though long since entered nirvāṇa, his whole body is undispersed, as though in meditation. I say he is no different from Prabhūtaratna. Even before the Master entered nirvāṇa he was no different from today. In that former time, Yongjia saw him once and at once realized the unborn, and though they pressed him to stay a single night, he could not be kept. Nanyue and Qingyuan both served him for more than ten years, and the various gates of samādhi they attained are beyond thought. Thus the light of buddhas and patriarchs shone forth like the clear sun rising in the sky; today the Way fills the world like the blazing sun of midsummer, and all who receive its warmth put out branches and send up trunks, bloom, and ripen into fruit, scattering again as diamond seeds beyond counting. All this is the merit of a single meeting with a good teacher. The keeper of the Caoxi stūpa attends upon the Master, washing and rinsing him morning and evening, serving tea, soup, and gruel no differently than when he was alive; at dawn and dusk the sound of bell and drum is the Master’s broad and long tongue blazing forth the Dharma without a moment’s pause, and those who attend him see and hear it morning and evening without a moment’s concealment. I wonder: among all you attendants, is there one who has realized the unborn like Yongjia? Is there one with the wondrous realization of Nanyue and Qingyuan? If so, then the udumbara flower has appeared for a time; if not, then the udumbara flower will never be seen. Since the good teacher is like the udumbara flower, then all you attendants who bow and draw near in offering through the six periods are engaged in the work of watering. Ah — the spiritual root is there, the seed of wisdom lies deep; if only the work of watering is complete and the conditions ripen, why fear that the udumbara will not appear at one time? The old man writes this in the Traveler’s Rest lodge and gives it to the keeper of the Caoxi stūpa, to keep as proof of the flower’s opening on another day.
Instruction to the Monks of Caoxi

Caoxi is the source of the Chan school’s vein throughout the world, and its mountains and rivers are the finest beyond the ridges; hence its monastery stands first among all places. Since the entry into nirvāṇa of Chan Master Dajian, the two elders Qingyuan and Nanyue put out branches and sent up trunks, sheltering gods and men everywhere: those who, in a word or half a phrase, in the raising of an eyebrow or the flicker of an eye, transcended birth and escaped death are beyond counting. Since then this mountain has lain silent for nearly a thousand years. Is it not that the branches grew great while the root was struck? Yet though its Way is said to be formless, it in fact lodges in form and rises and falls with the times — such is the principle. Seeking far back to the source of the five houses, their root is not two, and the purport of their founding also lies in responding to what is fitting. From Song to Yuan, elders such as Gaofeng, Duanya, and Zhongfeng all strove to rouse the family’s voice, and their lightning-like working was no less than in the monastery’s flourishing days. Since the rise of the Ming that wind has gradually declined; one dare not hope for true practice and real realization, and those with the will to go on the upward road are very few indeed. Elsewhere there may still be one or two who know this Way; but as for Caoxi, the true bone-and-blood descendants of the house, they alone do not know what a robe is or what shaving the head is for. Is it only men who have turned from the Way? Even the beauty of its mountains and rivers and the lushness of its monastery are no longer as they were then. And it has been invaded by evil demons and troubled in more ways than one. Is this not that its Way rises and falls with the times, and shares weal and woe with its mountains and rivers? In the spring of bingshen I received imperial grace and was sent to Leiyang. Passing by the mouth of Caoxi, I was able to pay my respects to the Sixth Patriarch. It happened to be just after the monks had finished their cooking, with the cauldrons still seething, and I shed tears for a long while before leaving. The next autumn Lord Chen, Grand Minister of War and Supreme Commander, mindful that Caoxi is the Zhu and Si of the Chan gate, wished to place me there to sweep and serve. At that time I was ashamed to be a blemish on the Dharma gate, and declined, fearing to disgrace the patriarchal seat. The year after, Lord Zhou Haimen, circuit inspector, governing Nan-Shao, was of one mind with Lord Chen, and though I firmly declined again and again, he had me put brush to paper and recompile the gazetteer. Lord Zhou left to present his congratulations at court, and Lord Zhu Xincun, the circuit inspector, took up office. He styled himself ‘the wandering monk of Caoxi,’ and within days of his arrival robbers were suppressed and lawsuits ceased, and the people enjoyed peace and harmony. At Caoxi’s gate a hundred neglected things were set right at once, as though Dajian had again taken up the corner of his robe. The monks who formerly neither knew nor understood all blazed forth the light of the Buddha-nature. Is this not ‘when a sentient being comes to plant the seed, the fruit is born again from the ground’? The Lord had long wished to obtain this humble one as an attendant to Dajian, hoping thereby to continue the merit of burning incense and washing bowls and to atone for the transgression of breaking the Dharma. For a long time I was ashamed. The Lord then left to present his congratulations; on the point of departure he had the monastery’s elders and the whole assembly bow, and first sent a letter and then gave repeated face-to-face admonitions, earnest to the last. I was moved that on this journey he did not count it a gain to hold office but rejoiced to become the master of Caoxi — is he not one who, at the door of illusion, manifests a magistrate’s body and performs the Buddha’s work? It must also be that the world’s way flourishes in accord, so that this mountain’s hues and this stream’s voice may thrust forth the Dharma body and utter the broad and long tongue. This humble body of sin and defilement dares not tread upon the jeweled flower or beat the poison drum; I merely write this to give to the monk who came, and to serve as a bond for entering the hall and attaining the room, as a condition for deliverance on another day. Written on the sixteenth day of the third month of the gengzi year.
Instruction to the Two Monastics Supervisors, Sulin Yu and Mu’an Tai of Caoxi

In the spring of bingshen I crossed the ridges and passed through Caoxi to pay my respects to the Sixth Patriarch. Gazing at his bodily remains as if alive, I thought how in those days he sat on the jeweled seat surrounded by a myriad fingers, no different from now; but today the halls and buildings are falling, the monastery is decayed, and the blessed ground of Baolin has become a lair of foxes and hares. I lingered long before leaving. Before many days the outer demons blazed up and the monks met with calamity. My heart grieved for them, so I sought out the magistrates in authority to be great protectors of the Dharma: Lord Chen, the supreme commander, and Lord Zhou of the grain and salt office both strove to revive it, and the demon wind gradually subsided — but the monks’ strength was utterly spent. At that time there were monks of the monastery such as Sulin Yu, Mu’an Tai, Haiyue Shan, and Jianchuan Shi, together with Xianghan Quan, who served as abbot of the restoration. These few all vowed to give up body and life, to uphold the Patriarch’s work with all their strength, to keep the assembly of monks safe, laboring day and night, worrying and planning with bitter hearts, seeking to be men who could give the patriarchal seat a single day’s shelter; their resolve was most earnest. Thereupon the community turned with sincerity, took refuge, and received the precepts, and asked me to enter the mountain. Imperial grace was still upon me, and I did not dare lightly consent; but though my body did not enter, my mind was already like diamond. In the jihai year of Wanli, Circuit Inspector Zhu of Nan-Shao, taking Caoxi upon his own shoulders, urgently commanded the assembly to invite me with ceremony. In the winter of gengzi I at last responded and entered the mountain; in less than three months a hundred neglected things were raised. I removed old corruption, selected monks, founded a school of instruction, and conferred the precepts, and in a single season all was transformed. I then laid out the design afresh and opened wide the Patriarch’s Way, and in less than five years the work was more than half complete. This was truly the Patriarch’s spirit working in silence and the dragons and gods protecting in the dark; and the single thought of blood-sincerity in men like Yu was in no way less than Shen Baoxu’s weeping in the Qin court. What true hearts and true practice call forth cannot be denied. I have dwelt here more than five years, and half of it has been spent in running about, all of it the toil of management; yet the community has served me as though it were the first day, even as I look upon the community as a single child. Lately I have received the imperial edict of pardon: though my body is not yet robed, my mind is already liberated. All the disciples were filled with joy, burned incense, bowed, and, holding scrolls, begged for words. So I took up my brush and instructed them: ‘Buddhas and sentient beings are one in mind, with no difference. The mind that is without difference is what is called the diamond mind-ground. This one mind the buddhas realized and thus taught the Dharma; the patriarchs awakened to it and thus saved beings; bodhisattvas cultivate it and thus accomplish the Way; the voice-hearers grasp it as nirvāṇa; the outsiders cling to it and slander the Dharma; sentient beings are deluded by it and create karma; the three evil paths are blind to it and suffer; ordinary men use it daily without knowing it; and we employ it in responding to conditions. You who are disciples of the Buddha and descendants of the Patriarch — whatever you do, all flows out from this mind. Only follow the teaching of buddhas and patriarchs and do the work of buddhas and patriarchs; let mind abide moment by moment and thought after thought never perish. Going on thus, uneroded through kalpas, this is the diamond mind-ground, the true causal seed of becoming a buddha and a patriarch. But if you oppose and turn your back on it, though your body wears the robe, your mind dwells in the path of karma; going on thus, this becomes the cause of suffering, and the bitter fruit of birth and death that does not perish through long kalpas. Hence it is said: “The dharmas above and below the three realms are made by one mind alone.” Follow it and you are a sage; turn from it and you are ordinary. Are these idle words? You few, Yu and the rest, share this mind, and the thousand men of the whole mountain share this mind as well. If you apply this mind to buddhas and patriarchs, it is diamond-like, and your future enjoyment will be diamond-like too. But if you apply it to your own single body, scheming for yourself alone and taking this little dung-heap as a land of bliss, your enjoyment will be like that of a suffering insect: thought after thought creating karma, and in the turning of an eye, before a single breath returns, you fall into the three evil paths, with endless bitter fruit and kalpa after kalpa, birth after birth, of enjoyment that is never exhausted. There is no other reason for this than that you do not understand that this mind is the true seed and field of blessing for becoming a buddha and a patriarch. Since I conferred the precepts on Yu, he has vowed to recite and uphold the Diamond Prajñā Sutra to the end of his life; and this sutra is the mind-ground of our Sixth Patriarch. If you can uphold it without forgetting and attain it for yourselves, then for kalpas to come your enjoyment will be inexhaustible, and this body and mind will abide forever at Caoxi. Hence it is said: “When a buddha-child dwells in this ground, that is the Tathāgata’s enjoyment; he ever abides therein, walking, sitting, and lying down.” You see clearly today that the old man has turned Caoxi into a Pure Land and driven the demon host to become companions in Dharma. If you believe in the wonder of this mind, then for all of you, escaping birth and death and realizing bodhi will take no more than a single thought. If not, you will drift on as before through the three evil paths and drown in the sea of suffering. Take this to heart!’
Instruction to the Novice Zhirong

By imperial grace I came south, and the Dharma protectors invited me to dwell at Caoxi. When I first entered the mountain, my first urgency was to nurture talent; so I selected novices, engaged a learned master to teach them, and had them practice their own calling — deportment, ritual, and recitation. I established a Chan hall for their dwelling and bound them by pure rules, and the community was as one finger. But the old man, drawn along by karmic conditions, could not dwell in peace; from time to time I taught them the Dharma and engaged a great elder of virtue to preside in my place. After several more years the design was complete and the monastery’s face was changed. The old man has often said that what the Buddhadharma values is that hearing and perfuming become seeds; Lingnan has long lacked the perfuming of Buddhadharma, and because seeds are lacking, faith is hard to bring forth. I have often vowed to have fifty-three monks each copy one copy of the great Avataṃsaka Sutra: first, because the vastness of the Dharma affinity makes it the supreme seed; second, because the power of copying and upholding supports the contemplation and practice of beginners and aids their provisions for entering the Way. Previously, flooded by inner demons, I had a vow unfulfilled. Among the community the novice Zhirong was the first to rouse his mind, vowing to copy the great sutra. The old man greatly admired his resolve. Before half the task of beginning the copying was done, the novices in charge of study all roused their minds at once, and there are now seven who are copying. Ah — how can men’s faculties be measured by a fixed rule? Long ago my teacher Śākyamuni, in a past kalpa, was an ordinary man when, together with a thousand men, he heard the names of fifty-three buddhas and all at once roused their minds to practice; afterwards each in turn became one of the thousand buddhas of the Bhadra kalpa, and my teacher, by the fierceness of his vow, was foremost among them. Again, as one of the sixteen princes, he heard the Lotus Sutra and made of it a causal seed of the One Vehicle, and in each of the eight directions attained buddhahood. How much more is the Avataṃsaka the great sutra of the One Vehicle, perfect and sudden, the Dharma realm of unobstructed dependent arising. It is said that in eight difficulties one leaps the stages of the ten grounds, and in one life one perfects the fruit of vast kalpas; one character embraces the sutra of the whole Dharma realm, and one practice contains the boundless ocean. How much more when dot by dot and stroke by stroke the light of mind streams forth and the great function appears before you. If the man of the moment is not blind to it, then he need not go further to consult koans, for contemplation and practice are complete in themselves; he need not journey afar through a hundred cities, for he sits and consults the good teacher. Is this not the supreme Dharma affinity? If the sutra you have copied stands before your eyes, and you recite, read, receive, and uphold it all your life, what other Buddhadharma would you seek? Even the seventeen hundred good teachers who flowed from the Sixth Patriarch’s transformation may all appear at once at the tip of a hair in the samādhi of a single stroke. You should contemplate in this way, and not let vulgar habit and the dust of defilement obstruct the eye of wisdom. Strive, strive!
Instruction to the Monastic Supervisor Fu Wu’ang of Caoxi

Though the trees of Deng Forest are many, few become timber; though the produce of the vast sea is abundant, few are called treasures. Confucius said, ‘Talent is hard to find’ — is it not so? Even of our Buddha’s forty-nine years of teaching, only the ten great disciples were each named foremost; and of the million gods and men who attained the treasury of the true Dharma eye, only Kāśyapa matched the mind. Through the ages those who transmit the Way and are called true bone-and-blood descendants are also not many. Our Sixth Patriarch taught the Dharma at Caoxi, and under his seat were no fewer than a thousand monks; the Platform Sutra records forty-three who awakened to the Way, yet those praised by name are only five or six, and of those who greatly spread his Way, only the two elders Nanyue and Qingyuan. Master Yue served the Patriarch with diligence, never leaving his side day or night for more than nineteen years, and with Qingyuan he shared his life until the Patriarch’s death. So from the first establishment of monasteries, whenever a good teacher opened the hall and taught, his business lay in gaining men, and he took the bitter hearts of these two elders as the family model. This is the difficulty of gaining men; and to seek one who can be a model for a hundred generations is harder still. When the old man first crossed the ridges and passed through Caoxi to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch, he saw the monastery’s gate in ruin, almost swept away, and the whole assembly trembling with nowhere to turn. So I vowed to revive the monastery and settle the community, to preserve the Patriarch’s threadlike line; and among a thousand monks I found five — Yu, Quan, Shi, Tai, and Shan — whose vow to have the old man as their refuge was like an infant’s longing for a loving mother, whose resolve to preserve the monastery was no less than Shen Baoxu’s resolve to preserve Chu, and whose pleading with me was no less than the weeping in the Qin court. So the old man, pitying their sincerity, came and took upon himself the burden of restoration; corruptions were pared away and a hundred affairs raised. I selected monks to learn ritual and recitation, and chose those fit to be models for the young and to be called teaching masters: three were found. Having placed them over months and years, and observed the subtlety of their intentions and the uprightness of their conduct, whether their words matched their deeds in forming later students to succeed former worthies and in minding the Patriarch’s Way and protecting the monastery, there was only one: the supervisor Ang. Among the three, who would not call himself their equal? Yet their conduct was not uniform, nor their resolve and practice equal; the weighing of light and heavy stood in men’s eyes and ears not for a day, plain as black and white. I have witnessed his conduct myself, and examined it as Confucius examined men, and not for a single day. So when the supervisors begged me for words, I gladly wrote at once; yet these three scrolls I kept for five years and did not lightly promise. It was not that I begrudged the Dharma. In the transmission between ancients and successors, one does not lightly give approval; for a single careless word may lose not only the man but the eye of the Dharma as well. The difficulty of knowing men afflicts even sages and wise men. It is said that the human heart is more perilous than mountains and rivers and harder to know than heaven; for heaven has the order of the four seasons, while man, with deep feelings and a solemn face, may carry a serpent and a tiger beneath his dignified bearing — he is not easily known. The saying goes: ‘In a fierce wind one knows the sturdy grass; in troubled times one knows the loyal minister.’ If everyone could be called loyal and filial, then the loyal ministers and filial sons of the world would be too many to be remarkable; because they are rare, their difficulty is seen; because it is difficult, to be a loyal minister or filial son is no easy thing. I have often said that Xuan Meng was praised for gaining scholars, yet those who risked death to preserve the orphan were only Cheng Ying and Chu Jiu; Chu was called rich in talent, yet he who gave up his life to restore Chu was Shen Baoxu alone. Ah — we who are śramaṇas and sons of Śākya: our flesh and blood, our liver and guts, are all transformed by buddhas and patriarchs; birth and death, rising and sinking, are also what buddhas and patriarchs rely on to turn. Those whose single mind is like that of the heroes of old are rare; for men love their karmic bodies and fashion implements of suffering, and are unwilling to fling body and life away with a willing heart. To seek one who in a single thought knows his fault and can embody the Patriarch’s family estate — such a man is hard to find. So we know: a house with no traitorous son is not ruined; a state with no treacherous minister is not destroyed; a man with no evil conduct does not perish; a scholar with no bitter practice does not make his name; goodness without adversity does not make its Way high; a mind without firm patience does not make its Way great. Thus we know that though good and evil differ, without the will of unshakable patience neither can be brought to reality; and if good and evil have no reality, their retribution cannot be relied upon for consistency. The saying goes: ‘Accumulated goodness brings fame; accumulated evil kills the body; accumulated water becomes the sea; accumulated earth becomes a mountain.’ If you, Ang, understand this, you need not worry that those evil men accumulate for themselves; you should worry that beneath your own body the loyal and steadfast work of the Way is not accumulated. Confucius said: ‘Do not worry that men do not know you; seek to be worthy of being known.’ Even if the Sixth Patriarch knew you had this mind, he would only say to you what the old man has said. Just strive — what other Dharma is there? To say more would only fall into the obstruction of proliferating words.
Instruction to the Monastic Supervisor Haiyue Shan of Caoxi

In the second month of spring in the bingshen year I passed through Caoxi and paid my respects to the Sixth Patriarch. I saw that incense and lamps were scant and the monastery was decayed, and I lingered long. A monk came forward with full deportment, bowed, and inquired after me with great respect. Seeing his sincerity and uprightness, I was pleased and said, ‘This is a true mountain monk.’ The next year, dingyou, the demon wind raged and this practice ground was nearly destroyed, and the monks had nowhere to turn. Master Shan and several of his fellows came to me at Wuyang and asked me to confer the precepts. Only then did I know that the one who had bowed before was Master Shan. In the winter of gengzi I answered the invitation and entered the mountain, and the Master led his disciples in attending the Patriarch’s stūpa. I observed the sincerity of his offerings, no different from when the Patriarch was alive, and sighed: ‘The patriarchal seat has stood a thousand years without decay, relying only on a single thought of filial reverence in its descendants.’ Hence the World-Honored One said, ‘Filial piety is called the precepts,’ just as in Confucianism filial piety is the root of benevolence: this is the root of the Way. When I dwelt in the mountain and first settled the summer retreat, whatever was undertaken came from the hearts of the many, yet Master Shan bore most of the toil and the resentment, his anxious diligence and careful reverence like that of a filial son toward a loving father, taking to heart every sorrow, joy, illness, and pain. So I knew his mind in serving the Patriarch was no different from his serving me. I therefore entrusted him with the permanent community, of one mind with the rest, giving himself wholly and forgetting his body for the Way. That the monastery is set in order again today and the Dharma’s transformation flourishes anew is surely the Patriarch’s spirit working in silence, yet it is truly what the filial sincerity of Shan and the rest called forth. The saying goes: ‘Unless the man is right, the Way does not walk in vain.’ I have often thought: had the Patriarch not embraced me, I could not have come to Caoxi; had I not come to Caoxi, it could not have today; and without the filial reverence of you and the rest, nothing could have bound my heart. The merit of restoring the monastery cannot, without pure sincerity, be brought to a full and complete end from first to last. It is altogether one great matter of affinity, and truly not accidental. Moreover, happily the building of the patriarchal seat is nearly complete; and on the twentieth day of the eighth month of bingwu I received the imperial edict permitting me to be a monk once more. Judging by this whole sequence, it is clear that I did not come without cause, nor did you come into this world and meet this affair without cause. Think how in the days when the Patriarch’s Way flourished greatly there were more than thirty disciples who awakened to the Way, while you were but sweepers and attendants; otherwise, how could you have the affinity to see me and draw near? Long ago, when the World-Honored One was with the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he taught the Lotus Sutra to his disciples, and in the end, down to the appearance of Śākyamuni, they came forth in the same assembly, each receiving a prediction of buddhahood. By the old affinity of former days and the present realization of today, then in the future, at Maitreya’s succession in the Dragon-Flower assembly, will one of you be lacking? Only hold fast to this mind, to glorify the Patriarch’s Way; take protecting the Three Jewels as your charge. Then a single stalk, a single leaf, a drop of water, a blade of grass or faggot — whatever benefits the monastery and supports the Dharma way — is a diamond seed and the true cause of buddhahood, so that for endless kalpas it is a refuge and the ten directions rely upon it; and you are one with the Patriarch’s Dharma body, abiding forever. How can you not strive?
Sent as Instruction to the Elders of Caoxi

While the old man dwelt at the patriarchal seat, all that he did was to unfold the one great matter of the Sixth Patriarch’s appearance in the world, wishing to lead everyone to cultivate the causes of transcendence and plant the conditions of the Pure Land. Unexpectedly the conditions went awry midway, the demon wind wrought destruction, and the lion’s worms made mischief, so that my original vow was not fulfilled; and in a single morning I parted far from the Patriarch and abandoned the great assembly. Even now, though I dwell on a lonely shore, not a single thought has forgotten my original vow. The younger students seem to have the will to go upward, but they bitterly lack a clear teacher and good friends to lead them onto the path of practice. Among the elders there are those who know the old man’s heart and deeply grieve over the great matter of birth and death, yet they have no old man to turn to and cannot gather in one place to do the Buddha’s work together. Alas, that days and months flow like water, that decay gradually encroaches, that the time of death draws near, and that on the road to the Yellow Springs their provisions are not ready — by what Dharma will they escape the bitter retribution of the three evil paths and the hells? To speak of this is pitiable and painful. The ancients said: ‘The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift; practice with utmost urgency — and even then you are already late.’ Therefore the old man has pondered again and again and has nothing by which to decide for the community. It happens that the hall master has come to visit, which exactly answers the old man’s heart. So I enjoin him earnestly: when he returns to the mountain, reveal the old man’s heart to the assembled elders. If any truly take birth and death to heart, let them all gather in one place, form a Buddha-recitation society, cultivate pure practice together, and together escape birth and death, vowing to deliver one another in turn. If one in the society should pass away first, let all aid him with one strength to be reborn in the Pure Land. Is this not the first and most supreme affinity? Even this remaining life would then surpass a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives spent in vain. The place of meeting must above all be pure and undisturbed, so that the work of the Way can be accomplished. The Chan hall has only the younger students’ recitation, and its business seems busy and mixed; only the Wujin Hermitage that the old man built is utterly still, with everything ready to hand. It would be better to make this the hall of pure practice and accomplish a surpassing matter — thus not only would the old man’s bitter heart not be spent in vain, but the merit of the donors would be repaid. As for the rules of practice, the ancients recited the Buddha’s name at six periods, diligent day and night; though this is vigorous, I fear the elderly cannot manage it, so let four periods be the standard: two periods for the regular service, and two periods kneeling to recite one fascicle of the Chapter on the Conduct and Vows, with a thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name and the making of vows and dedication. Let the term have no fixed limit and the number of people no fixed count, but require only that they be mature, of firm faith, and genuine: forgetting host and guest, effacing self and other, cutting off right and wrong, abstaining from frivolous talk, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name, receiving no guests, and taking stillness as the master — this is the true forest hermitage, the place of right practice. If the community can truly see the old man’s heart, believe his words, and practice according to the Dharma, then this is the season for escaping birth and death; then you will be with the old man life after life and birth after birth, never parted, ever born before the Buddha and hearing the sound of the Dharma together. As for the persons who form the society and the place of dwelling, let all be decided by the hall master: this is to carry out the old man’s instruction. As for the work of the Way and its vigor, that lies with the community, each striving for himself. The ancients said: ‘You cannot walk for another by taking his hand; only when a man himself consents is it truly near.’ It is said that if only you rouse the consenting mind, you will surely not be cheated. Treasure this and strive.
Sent as Instruction to the Disciples of the Caoxi Chan Hall

When the old man first undertook the building for the Patriarch, the community did not know his heart. Now that the old man has gone, you all take pleasure in entering the hall and dwelling there in peace, whatever the fortunes of the monastery and the founding of the Chan hall — so you know the old man’s bitter heart. If you know the old man’s heart, you should know the hearts of buddhas and patriarchs. You now think that you might obtain the old man’s former instruction, but you cannot. Yet though buddhas and patriarchs cannot escape the conditions of meeting and parting, if disciples can know their grace and repay it by practicing according to the teaching, then even after a buddha’s nirvāṇa it is no different from drawing near him in life. So when the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, the great disciples asked: after the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, what shall the community take as teacher? The Buddha said: ‘Reverence the Prātimokṣa; it is your great master.’ Prātimokṣa in Sanskrit means ‘precepts.’ The Buddha often said: ‘You monks, if you can keep my precepts, then though you are a thousand miles away, you are at my side; if you do not revere my precepts, then though face to face, you are a thousand miles apart.’ These are the words personally entrusted by our master the Buddha with his golden mouth — how can we not follow them? Moreover, in this Dharma-ending age we are far from the sage’s time; if disciples of the Buddha do not uphold the Buddha’s precepts, on what ground will they practice, and by what will they escape the bitter sea of birth and death? When the old man was about to depart he especially expounded the Brahma Net Precepts for you. I do not know whether each of you can firmly uphold them. The Buddha ordained that monks should recite this precept sutra every half month, as though hearing the Buddha himself perform the karma, allowing no breach; let the three karmas and six senses be examined and observed thought by thought, allowing no hidden transgression, no breach of the root of the precepts. This itself is true practice; sitting and advancing in this Way, you need not seek out a clear teacher far away and merely add to your toil. If you have not been able to uphold them firmly until now, then from today follow the Dharma: every half month, before the Buddha, recite aloud the Brahma Net Precept Sutra — the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts, each rule memorized distinctly. If you break one, then on the day of recitation ask the master of discipline to witness, let the community examine one another in turn, and let the offender confess before the assembly and never offend again. Thus you reform and renew yourselves, and the work of the Way can be accomplished. As for the offenses committed, besides confession, let the community agree on pure rules and penalties for compliance. The revised rules the old man left in former days may serve as standing law. When the community is familiar with the precept sutra, you should recite from memory the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters, the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching Sutra, the Śūraṅgama, Lotus, and Laṅkāvatāra sutras, as seeds of buddhahood. As for the one matter of Chan inquiry, follow the Sixth Patriarch’s instruction to Huiming: ‘Think neither good nor evil — at such a moment, what is your original face?’ Keep this koan in your breast and investigate it at all times; in time it will surely open. Thus alone is the great matter of continuing the wisdom-life of buddhas and patriarchs. If you can follow these words, then the old man abides forever at Caoxi, and you need not wander with your staff from place to place.
Instruction to the Novices of Caoxi

In the gengzi year those in authority invited me to set Caoxi in order. I consented; but when I arrived, a hundred neglected things could not all be raised. Reflecting that the way of governance takes the nurturing of talent as its root, I selected novices, founded a school of instruction, and engaged guest masters to teach them deportment and to read the inner and outer classics. When they had some knowledge of faith and direction, they were shaved and a Chan hall was established, where they lived by pure rules, received the precepts, and bowed and recited day and night. At that time the novices first came to know that there is a calling in leaving home, and all wearied of ploughing and digging and longed for pure practice. I labored bitterly for ten years, and there was some little to show; then I abandoned it and left. Now I am old and dwell in retirement at Nanyue. The novices who once received my teaching did not deeply know the old man then; now they think of him deeply. Yet to obtain a single day of attendance or a single word of instruction is hard. One novice was then a small child; now, among the community, he has first come to know the old man, and longing to draw near in his heart but unable, he has sent a register and begged instruction from afar. Hearing of it, the old man was both grieved and glad. Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world, fearing that by dwelling long he would make the faithless among beings hold him lightly, he ascended to Trāyastriṃśa, letting the community long for him and then return, so that each would cherish the thought of how hard it is to meet him. Had the old man dwelt long at Caoxi, how could you have longed for him as you do today? If a novice would think of the old man, better to think of the Buddha and think of the Sixth Patriarch. If you think of the Buddha, in the future you will surely see the Buddha; and to see the Buddha is to escape birth and death. Think of the Sixth Patriarch: at first he was only a woodcutter; how did he come to receive the offerings of gods and men today? Think again of today’s offerings: they came from casting off his mother’s love, going to Huangmei’s assembly, carrying stones and pounding rice, and bitter toil. Think again of the Sixth Patriarch: at the third watch he entered Huangmei’s abbot’s quarters and received the robe and bowl — by what insight, among five hundred men, did he alone obtain them? And every man has a stinking skin bag that within three or five days of death rots unbearably; why is the Sixth Patriarch’s body, after a thousand years, as though alive? What manner of practice yields such firmness and indestructibility? If a novice ponders all this carefully, point by point, and cannot penetrate it, then simply read the Platform Sutra over and over and investigate it closely, again and again. If you cannot manage the whole, then take just the one line, ‘Originally there is not a single thing — where can dust alight?’ and keep it in your breast. Walking, standing, sitting, lying, drinking tea, eating, carrying firewood, hauling water, greeting guests, receiving visitors — through the six periods of the day, in every place, raise it to mind at every turn, until before your eyes you must see just what this ‘originally not a single thing’ is, and what is the state in which no dust alights. If you can apply your mind thus, it is called Chan inquiry. If you investigate to the place where you yourself believe without doubt, then you can truly see the Sixth Patriarch’s face, and only then will you know the old man’s nostrils; only then is a novice truly leaving home and the season of escaping birth and death. If you refuse to seek the fundamental matter bitterly within your own mind, then to think of the old man in vain — what benefit is there? Formerly the novices knew only how to receive the old man’s teaching in person, practicing only deportment and movement and reciting texts. But from today, let what the novices have requested be instructed thus: put all your strength into the work, and only then is it the old man’s true instruction. The old man is old; this is his last instruction. If you miss today, then in the future, though you travel the ten directions to consult teachers, it will always be another man’s business. Be careful not to take the old man’s words as idle talk.
Instruction to Fakong, the Selected Hall Master

The Buddha taught disciples of the Dharma-ending age to practice the four peaceful practices — right body, right speech, right mind, and great compassion — and to cultivate according to these is called wondrous practice. In these four practices, the place of practice and the place of nearness are the beginner’s starting point: the place of practice means not straying from the practice ground step by step; the place of nearness means not straying from the Three Jewels thought by thought. I observe that among monks of the Dharma-ending age, those who can tread these practices are closest to it in the duty of tending the shrine hall. For śramaṇas and sons of Śākya who do not know the essentials of practice, who let body and mind run wild and cannot discipline the three karmas, every movement becomes an offense, so that the karma of sin deepens daily and birth and death are hard to escape. Even one who can travel far to consult teachers cannot necessarily follow them step by step and draw near them mind to mind. Only in serving the Three Jewels is one not forgetful of the Buddha: incense and lamps by day and night. In assembling the community at dawn and dusk for bell, drum, and recitation, one is not forgetful of the Dharma. In the community’s harmony and its comings and goings through the six periods, one is not forgetful of the Saṅgha. Sitting, lying, walking, standing without leaving the Buddha hall — that is the practice ground at every step. If one can purify one’s own mind, then a single stick of incense and a single flower all become the Buddha’s true substance, and every raising of the hand and bowing of the head is wondrous practice. Thus without moving the heels one consults every teacher — is this not the most supreme affinity? There is no peaceful wondrous practice higher than this. Let the practitioner strive to the end of his life; what other Buddhadharma is there to seek?
Instruction to Ji, the Estate Master of Caoxi

When the Sixth Patriarch dwelt at Baolin in Caoxi he could not accommodate a large assembly, so he begged from the villager Chen Yaxian a patch of ground the size of his robe, and it covered the whole of Caoxi’s four boundaries; the Zisun estate on the mountain’s back was one corner of that robe. Formerly monks’ quarters occupied half the monastery there. In time the monks forgot their root, outside insults gradually encroached, and the powerful nibbled away at it, so that most of the mountain land and fields passed into the hands of the strong; eight or nine tenths of the monks’ estate was lost, and the whole spine of the Patriarch’s dragon was gone. The local people cut firewood as far as the inner lands, and the encroachment was about to reach the very armpits. When the old man first entered Caoxi he learned the whole story and said to the community: ‘Land is the root of a monastery. Moreover our Patriarch’s robe is still the same, and Yaxian’s ancestral grave still stands; this is what is called the old Patriarch’s field. How can it be lost?’ So he gathered the community and appealed to the supreme commander, who ordered the prefecture to clear the old lands and set the boundaries right. The community was all at a loss, not knowing where the limits lay; and those who did know shrank back and said nothing. Only Master Ji, having lived there formerly, could point out every detail; and so the power of the strong was checked. The old man then raised funds and redeemed the former fields, mountain lands, and woodlands, giving them all to support the Baolin Chan hall and maintain the monastery’s younger monks who were willing to undertake the work of the Way — to redeem the Sixth Patriarch’s threadlike line. He accordingly made Master Ji estate master. Master Ji assisted the old man in restoring Caoxi, setting in order the permanent endowment’s money and grain and all its affairs, everything neat and well ordered. If this can be maintained, a thousand years will be as a single morning. Since the old man left Caoxi nearly ten years have passed, and all the rules have fallen into disuse; only the Chan hall has been kept by Master Ang as before, while Master Ji, the estate master, keeps a pure and single heart and has not forgotten his first resolve, looking upon the old man as though he were at his side, and protecting the permanent endowment in every least thing as he would his own eyes. The old man is ashamed that he has no affinity to fulfill the Patriarch’s Way to the full. And I reflect that long ago Huanglong wore a look of displeasure, and when the chief seat asked him why, he answered: ‘We have not found the right man for the superintendent of receipts.’ So we know that the ancients gave such deep thought even to appointing a single superintendent. How much more is the estate master’s charge no small matter? From ancient times states have found it hard to get the right men, and so it is with monasteries. Of Caoxi’s thousand monks, after the old man had dwelt there ten years sifting them, he found only one Chan hall master and one estate master — two men. With two or three more who could serve as their wings, then virtue would not stand alone, affairs would be easily carried out, and the Patriarch’s practice ground could be kept free of anxiety. The hall master has come to visit the old man at Mount Kuang, and Master Ji sends this scroll by him to ask for instruction. What more can the old man say? Our Buddha’s appearance in the world had no other business than these two matters: protecting in mind and entrusting. What he protects in mind is the wish to gain men, to continue the wisdom-life; what he entrusts is the family estate of the Buddha, given over to another, as an elder gives his estate into his son’s hands. So all the patriarchs through the ages have been of the Buddha’s mind, their will set on the wisdom-life never being cut off. Now the Way of buddhas and patriarchs is lodged in the single line of Caoxi, and Caoxi’s business lies in gaining men. Gaining men depends on maintenance, and maintenance depends on the four requisites, and the four requisites depend on the one in charge. If the one in charge is the right man, then the community has somewhere to turn, the Way can be accomplished, the monastery can be revived, and the Dharma way can flourish. When the Dharma way flourishes and benefits, the wisdom-life of buddhas and patriarchs continues unbroken forever into the future — and this depends entirely on today. To protect the wisdom-life is to repay the Buddha’s grace deeply; this is what it means to be truly a child of the Buddha. Master Ji may be said to have repaid the Patriarch’s grace and virtue. If from today he can further keep the Sixth Patriarch deeply in mind — the koan of his teaching Huiming on the ridge of Dayu — hold it in his breast, plant doubt again, doubt on and on until doubt can go no further, and suddenly the mass of doubt bursts open and his original face appears: then he may be called a true bone-and-blood descendant of the Sixth Patriarch. Compared with protecting the old Patriarch’s fields, this may be called advancing a step beyond the top of a hundred-foot pole. This koan is the Sixth Patriarch’s lifeline. If one man penetrates it, then the Sixth Patriarch abides forever in the world and has not entered nirvāṇa. Now this thousand-year-old stale antique the old man has taken up and brought out again, and through you its value is raised; henceforth it will ever shine, lighting heaven and earth. You should stake this body and life on it, make your mind firm, and not be slack for a single breath. Strive!

Instruction to Ang, Hall Master of Baolin at Caoxi

Lingnan first opened communication with China in the Han, and only then knew of civilization: more than six hundred years. In the early Tang the Sixth Patriarch rose in Xinzhou, received the robe and bowl of Huangmei, and transmitted the direct-pointing Way that came from the West; only then did men know there was a Buddhadharma. He opened the Baolin practice ground at Caoxi and taught the Dharma there. From that time the Way’s shade spread over the world, and the whole Chan school took this as its beginning. How flourishing it was! After the Sixth Patriarch’s nirvāṇa his bodily form remained, but the practice ground gradually declined; and by the Song, after more than three hundred years, the monastery was in utter ruin. At that time Chan Master Zichao rose up and greatly revived it, and so its Way flourished again. Yet of those recorded in the lamp transmission, after the Sixth Patriarch few are seen. So though the Dharma spread through the ten directions, those who gave their hearts to the root ground were few. With no master to open and transform it, the monks took up worldly trades and forgot their root altogether — a matter of course. From Song down to the Wanli era of our Ming is nearly five hundred more years, and the ruin of the practice ground is even worse than in Song: the monks could not dwell there, and the Dharma cavern was inhabited by foxes and hares. In the bingshen year the old man came beyond the ridges and was able to pay his respects at the patriarchal seat; seeing its unbearable condition, he left with his heart deeply pained. Five years later, in gengzi, the Dharma protectors, all with the Dharma way at heart, urgently wished the old man to go and save it from its ills. On arriving he made a vow, giving up body and life, resolved to be a loyal minister and filial son of the Sixth Patriarch. In a single season all was renewed and a hundred neglected things raised — this was by the power of the buddhas’ and patriarchs’ protecting care, not by human strength. At that time the monks numbered a full thousand, and those who feared the community would not be at peace were only a few; but of those who grieved that the Patriarch’s Way was not revived, that later students had no eye, that the Dharma banner was not firm, there was only Ang. And as for knowing the old man’s resolve to restore and his will to die for it, only you. Ah — so hard is it for the Dharma gate to gain men. At that time, when the old man first entered Caoxi, he selected the monks and taught those who could be taught; and in searching the community, again only you. During the eight years the old man dwelt here, whatever was planned for the monastery’s long future was beyond the community’s grasp; and what his heart touched and took in, great and small without omission, was again only you. And when the lion’s worms broke the Dharma and the demon host strove together, even those few formerly called the practice ground’s pillars were all caught in the net, with no leisure to seek escape. One who with bitter heart protected the monastery, grieved that the Patriarch’s Way was splitting, and deeply knew the old man’s grace in building it — again only you alone. At that time, had you not stood as a pillar in midstream and patiently sheltered it, Caoxi would never have had today. And when the old man abandoned it and left, the Chan hall had no master and was nearly devoured by the lion’s worms; had you not thrust yourself forward to hold it up, not only would the practice ground have been destroyed and later students left with no support, but the old man’s whole bitter heart of restoration would have been poured down the drain. How then could one hope for the Patriarch’s Way to revive? So since the old man parted from Caoxi, ten years now, you have thought bitterly day and night of his return, hoping the Dharma way would be renewed, grief in every thought, never forgetting for a single breath. The old man went to Nanyue and you followed; then the old man retired at Mount Kuang, and you soon came from afar. I see your gratitude deepening and your grief for the Way growing daily, as you long for the old man’s return or hope for the coming of a true man. Such sincerity is hard to describe in words; even the loyal ministers and filial sons of old who grieved for state and family, the chaste women and widows who vowed death with no second heart, do not surpass it. You have come to the mountain and the old man has kept you long. Your sorrowing heart asks instruction without end. So the old man instructs you: ‘Your resolve is indeed admirable, but your thinking is excessive. Have you not heard that when the great Way declines, even buddhas and patriarchs cannot escape the conditions of the times? The meeting of conditions does not come from human strength. Moreover the Way rises and falls with the fortunes of the age and can hardly be forced; and the right man is not easily found either. Look closely: since the Sixth Patriarch’s nirvāṇa a thousand years have passed. His Way fills the world; in every monastery it opens and transforms no small number. But of those who manage the family rule for the patriarchal seat, only Zichao of Song. After Zichao, another five hundred years: of those whose will was set on the Patriarch’s Way and who by strength set the fallen order right, only the old man. And at Caoxi, among a thousand men, of those who grieve for the Patriarch’s Way and know the old man, only you. So how rarely is a man of the Dharma gate who takes this to heart! Now the old man shows you the most supreme Dharma gate: what is called “seeking a man is not as good as seeking yourself.” When the Sixth Patriarch had not yet appeared in the world he was only a woodcutter; because he had planted a spiritual root in former lives and his practice had long been matured, in a single morning, hearing one phrase of the sutra, he suddenly awakened to his own mind and so obtained the robe and bowl of Huangmei. Was not today’s Baolin practice ground born from the Sixth Patriarch’s shoulder-pole and rice-pounding, from the stone at his waist? Hence such vast radiance covering heaven and earth. Every word and phrase of the Chan school flowed out from the carrying pole and the waist-stone; and even now the offerings of incense and fire are no different from when he was alive, his bodily form firm and indestructible, no different from teaching in the present. Such blessing too came from the carrying pole and the waist-stone. How could it have been obtained by deliberately seeking a man? Since you have the resolve to grieve over the Patriarch’s Way on high, why must you seek a man to answer it? “He being a great man, so am I.” The one stretch of prajñā light the Sixth Patriarch awakened to is shared by everyone, lacking not a hairsbreadth. Now you should grieve only that your own mind is not awakened, not that the practice ground is not revived. If you can awaken to your own mind, then you can churn the long river into cream, turn the great earth into gold, pick up a blade of grass and make it a sixteen-foot golden body, and take a sixteen-foot golden body and make it a blade of grass, naturally possessing great spiritual powers, transforming at will, acting as you please, nothing not permissible. Thus it all lies complete within me — why then think so bitterly and foolishly, hoping another will come and do my family’s work? The ancients who wished to awaken their own minds: before the Sixth Patriarch, all awakened at a single word in the present moment, and there was no talk of doing practice. From the Sixth Patriarch’s receiving the robe and bowl of Huangmei, his koan on the ridge of Dayu instructing the Daoist Huiming became the model of doing practice and inquiring into Chan ever after. From now on, let me have you cast aside at once all your former worrying about long and short and your mind of looking to others. Only put down body and mind yourself, stake your one life, and with a single thought seek only to awaken clearly to your own mind. Lay the koan of Huiming across your breast, plant doubt again, and through the six periods of day and night, walking, standing, sitting, lying, greeting guests, receiving visitors, handling affairs, meeting things, in tea and in food, lifting spoon and raising chopsticks — let nothing be let go. Doubt on and on until you must see your own original face. Or take up the huatou of Buddha-recitation and ask: who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? What is he, after all? Doubt thus until it is like a mountain of silver and a wall of iron; and at the point where doubt can go no further, suddenly the root of life is severed, the mass of doubt bursts, and your own original face appears at once. Then you will know the one who recites the Buddha, like meeting your own father in the crossroads. No need to ask anyone else. The ancients said: “One who is good at carving out the Way needs a thousand days’ work.” Some take ten years, some five, some twenty or thirty, and some do not awaken in a whole life and vow to come forth again; some take two lives, three lives, or even ten and many lives, not losing their original vow. Birth and death are long, and in the everlasting quiet light there is no trace of coming or going. Moreover your years and strength are still strong. If you can truly decide, begin from today; if you can awaken in ten or twenty years, you will still have fulfilled my original vow in this life. Even if you do not awaken now, relying on this work of inquiry and the seeds of prajñā, when you come forth again it will still be a living trade. Even at the longest, no more than forty or fifty years — a somersault, and it is as if before your eyes. To set your own household in order then, what difficulty is there? To neglect this and worry about other things is all wasted thought; deluded thinking brings no benefit. Not only no benefit, it adds to the boundless bitter sea of birth and death. Is this not great folly? The old man’s words are like a club striking a stone man’s head. To do the work thus is to have the old man constantly between your brows, emitting light and shaking the earth.’
Instruction to Rong, Hall Master of the Pilgrims’ Lodge at Caoxi

The monasteries of the world are resting places for the wandering monks of the ten directions who travel on foot, roaming ten thousand miles amid clouds, climbing mountains, braving wind and rain, treading snow and ice, enduring hunger and cold and hardship, their shadows for company on the long road, with nowhere to know rest. So they look to a monastery for a single night’s peace, like a poor son looking to his parents’ house. But if in some place the one in charge is not the right man, and indifferent, gives no thought, so that the hungry get no food, the thirsty no drink, the weary no rest, the sick no comfort — then to whom can their hearts, so bleak and afflicted, complain? From ancient times the establishing of monasteries to receive the ten directions has been deeply mindful of this. In other quarters, with roads in four directions, there are always alternatives; or there are neighboring peaks and market towns where one may find lodging, or go elsewhere. But as for the Caoxi practice ground in Lingnan, where the Sixth Patriarch’s flesh body still exists and which every wandering monk in the realm must visit and revere: those who come must travel thousands of miles, crossing the ridges for this single purpose, braving lands of miasmic vapors and coming out of a place of nine deaths to one life, arriving with blistered feet. Can there be no provision here for receiving them? Before the old man came to Caoxi, I heard that when monks arrived there was no peaceful lodging to rest their shoulders, and they could not obtain a single drink or meal. They all went about begging, and the monks’ quarters were shut against them; and if they got a pint or a peck of rice, there was no place to cook it, so they gathered firewood by the stream, or ate once and went on. The old man grieved over this, and so he cleared away the slaughterhouses and wine shops and made of the place a Chan hall for receiving the ten directions, establishing a separate kitchen so that they might eat; all that was needed was supplied from the inner hall, and always made sufficient. He let the hungry eat, the thirsty drink, the weary rest, the sick be nursed, the dirty wash; he let them stay long or short, come and go as they would. Thus a sea of karma became a land of bliss. But to find the right man for the post is not easy, and there are those who make of it a hell — plenty of them. Or lion’s worms gather here to work demonic obstruction, and those who cannot control them mostly have no peace. Lately Master Ang came and said that he had found Master Rong as master of the pilgrims’ hall, and everything was fitting, fully answering the intention of the founding. He has served three years as a single day. The old man heard it and said with joy: ‘This is where the old man’s vow has reached.’ I have often thought that a bodhisattva’s practice takes the comforting of beings as its root: one should regard all beings — the old as fathers, the young as brothers — and serve them with a filial heart. How much more in the Dharma gate, where there is the bond of one body, unlike any other. If one can serve them with a filial heart, then one takes the Buddha’s mind as one’s own mind. The Brahma Net Precept Sutra is the Buddha’s mind-ground Dharma gate; it first declares that filial piety is called the precepts — filial reverence toward the Three Jewels, filial reverence toward teachers and monks, filial reverence toward the Dharma of the utmost Way. If one can receive these precepts, one enters the rank of all buddhas. Thus filial reverence is the root of the precepts, and the precepts are the root of buddhahood. To practice this practice is the foundation of becoming a buddha; there is no need to seek other Buddhadharma. The Avataṃsaka Sutra says: when a bodhisattva gives to beings head, eyes, body, flesh, hands, and feet, if a beggar comes he gives at once and goes with him, and congratulates himself, saying: “Those who come begging are all my good teachers, friends uninvited, who can accomplish for me immeasurable merit and make firm my bodhi vow.” From this we see that all who come today from the ten directions are my friends uninvited. If Master Rong can serve and make offerings with a filial heart, filling the diamond precepts as seeds of buddhahood, then this one practice wholly contains all practices; why abandon this for some other mysterious Buddhadharma? If Master Rong can truly believe the old man, and from now on with deep heart to the end of his life make offerings to the ten directions with firm resolve never retreating, then he is a bodhisattva giving beings head, eyes, hands, and feet, no different at all; and in seeking the Buddha’s wondrous Way, what could be added to this?
