If not, then take the Sixth Patriarch’s one phrase, “originally there is not a thing,” and lay it across your breast; in time, once you recognize your own original face, then you will string the Sixth Patriarch’s nostrils on one thread, and see that picking up a blade of grass is already building a monastery — and you will only fear that the clouds and waters of the ten directions do not arrive sooner, so how could there be weariness? Alas, I am old, and ashamed that I cannot again be a servant of the Sixth Patriarch. If you can embody this, you will be turning this same Dharma wheel for the old man always.
Instruction to the Caoxi Novice Dayi

The old man has retired at Mount Kuang. Master Ang, hall master of Baolin, brought the novice Dayi a long way to pay his respects. The old man instructed him: ‘You should consider by what practice and what merit you were born in a border land, yet became a descendant of the Sixth Patriarch, drawing near his flesh body morning and evening as though he were teaching in the present — and how utterly foolish you are, like one born blind who does not know that the sunlight shines on him. By what affinity and what fortune did you obtain the old man’s coming, to scrape the film from your eyes with a golden lancet, open your blindness, and let you first see the light of sky and sun — and still you do not know the sunlight shines on you. You should reflect that before the Sixth Patriarch went to Huangmei he was only a woodcutter of Xinzhou; hearing the one phrase of the Diamond Sutra, “should produce a mind nowhere abiding,” he suddenly cut off the root and stalk of birth and death through countless kalpas. Was this because of training and instruction? Truly, the seed of the Buddha-nature is complete in everyone; only, not meeting the condition to open it, it is like a seed in the ground that has not received the moisture of rain and dew. The old man has always pointed directly for you in every kind of expedient: all of it is the work of rain. But your afflictions are deep-rooted, and the numinous sprout of the seed of wisdom is hard to bring forth. That you have come from afar to ask instruction is still the work of former watering. From now on, if you would have the seed of wisdom spring up, take the one phrase the Sixth Patriarch awakened to — “no abiding” — and grasp it and investigate it. Suddenly the mind-ground will open, and then not only will you finish with birth and death through kalpas, but the Sixth Patriarch’s nostrils will be wholly in your hands: holding them fast and letting them go will be up to yourselves. Then you will be no different from attending the Sixth Patriarch in person as he teaches the Dharma — why wait for the old man to beat around the vines and spend a grandmother’s heart? Though the old man is not at Caoxi, you need only tell this one koan of the house to your fellow novices: everyone must do the work thus, and not let it go for a single thought. Thus the old man abides forever on this mountain and teaches the Dharma for you all at every moment. This matter is no child’s play; it requires a single dead-set mind, a poisoned hand, staking your life’s root, and doing it. If you are three in the morning and four in the evening, one day cold and ten days hot, not only will the seed of wisdom not grow, I fear it will become a scorched sprout and a rotten seed. Then you will have failed not only the old man but truly failed yourselves. Above all do not let the time pass in vain, lest when the great limit comes and this human body is lost, it cannot be recovered for ten thousand kalpas. You should think deeply and encourage yourselves. Do not be careless.’
Instruction to the Caoxi Novice Fangjue

Bodhidharma came from the West, singly transmitting the direct-pointing Way; the robe and bowl passed through six generations to Caoxi, and the treasury of the true Dharma eye spread through China. Now more than a thousand years have passed, and all speak of the single line of Caoxi, like the Zhu and Si rivers of Confucius’s school — the Dharma gate depends on it heavily. When I formerly dwelt in the Eastern Sea, I often lamented that the Chan gate was desolate and that the source must be choked; I once discussed with Master Daguan going to dredge it, and we set a time at Mount Kuang. Before long I met with calamity for spreading the Dharma, and Master Da, thinking I would not go, went alone first; arriving at the mountain, he saw that the monks were all farmhands, and he stopped beneath the eaves, lodged two nights, and returned. Soon after, I too met with calamity for spreading the Dharma and was sent by imperial grace beyond the ridges. At the time I took it to be the buddhas’ and patriarchs’ spiritual power drawing me. The Master waited for me on the river and said to me: ‘I went ahead and explored Caoxi; even if the Sixth Patriarch were born again, it could not be revived.’ I said: ‘It depends on the strength of one’s vow.’ When I crossed the ridges and had dwelt there five years, in gengzi, those in office, with Caoxi’s protection at heart, urgently brought me there. On arriving I began with the patriarchal seat and the various gates, raising a hundred neglected things at once. As for the monks, great and small, and even the novices, they were all woodcutters’ and herdsmen’s boys; so I built a separate Chan hall and set up pure rules, having each follow his own calling. There were more than a hundred such. Alas that their affinity with prajñā was not deep: though the old man earnestly showed them the great principles of the Buddhadharma, few took them up — it stopped at deportment. The old man labored bitterly for eight years, and when the icchantika monks made trouble he at last took his leave for Nanyue. The novices, like infants deprived of milk, followed one after another without cease. Attendant Jue first waited for me at Nanyue, and now waits at Mount Kuang, and so he takes up incense and asks instruction. The old man, grieving, said to him: ‘You were born in a border land and have not heard the names of the Three Jewels: that is one difficulty. Happily you met the old man to open and guide you — what fortune! Though you have the affinity to receive teaching, in the end you cannot enter deeply into the Buddhadharma: it is that you have not planted the affinity of prajñā. That you remember me without forgetting shows the root of faith is present, and the Buddhadharma will enter in time. It is said that to know the meaning of the Buddha-nature one should observe the conditions of the time. Now that you know to leave worldly entanglements and stand free beyond the world, this is the right cause for entering the Way. And you have drawn near a teacher and know how hard it is — so you should not let deluded and wild thoughts pass the matter by face to face; this is to know what is weighty. If, having left worldly conditions, you think yourself free of restraint, let body and mind run wild, occupy yourself with empty splendor, dally with mountain and water, and merely wear out straw sandals — what benefit is there? Will you not only add to the suffering of karma? If you can truly stake body and life, resolve to seek the great Dharma, take the great matter of birth and death as your aim, investigate the upward road, and while your strength and vigor are strong, for twenty or thirty years seek only to awaken to your own nature and not stop until you do — such resolve is the right practice of one who has left home. Then you will not fail the old man’s grace in guiding you, nor fail the affinity of meeting a good teacher through a thousand lives and ten thousand kalpas, nor fail your leaving home and drawing near the Sixth Patriarch’s flesh body, no different from when he was alive. You must further make a vow: a vow to spread the Patriarch’s Way, to save the practice ground, to preserve the standard of the Dharma gate. To set your mind and resolve thus is to be a true bone-and-blood descendant of Caoxi. But if you spend the days idly, clinging to your own folly, taking pilgrimage to famous mountains and reverence at the patriarchal seat and rejoicing in the practice ground as the whole matter — that is the way of the rice-gruel rabble, the lowest of men. Though you travel all the famous mountains, you will remain a worldly-boned, ordinary-fleshed man with not the slightest gain; will you not then fail your own great affinity of a hundred thousand kalpas? Think it over carefully; be careful not to ruin yourselves.’
Colophon to the Avataṃsaka Sutra Copied by My Disciple Chaoyi

This is the colophon I wrote in the first month of winter in the renyin year, on Mount Baotuo, for my disciple Chaoyi, who copied out the Avataṃsaka Sutra to complete it for his fellow disciple Shixing, recounting the whole course of his rousing the mind. Since I received imperial grace and crossed the ridges, teaching the Dharma at Wuyang and instructing for several years, of those in black robes who firmly believed and took refuge there were only a few beneath the bodhi tree; and among those few only Master Yi and Shixing, two men, shared one resolve and one practice, together rousing the great mind to copy the great Dharma-nature. Before it was half done Shixing died young, and only Yi completed the work. Ah — not only is rousing the mind hard; even having roused it, to have the conditions and fulfill the vow is harder still. Hence our World-Honored One, in the assemblies, repeatedly spoke of how hard it is to have faith in the Dharma: as when he said, ‘Though a man should carry dry grass into a world consumed by fire and not be burned, that is not hard; but after my nirvāṇa, to uphold this sutra and expound it for one man — that is hard.’ From this we see that it is not only faith in the Dharma that is hard; upholding the Dharma is harder by ten thousand times. Moreover this southern Yue lies at the sea’s edge, its customs far from the central land; the Buddhadharma began when Bodhidharma crossed the sea and once rested at Wuyang, and Master Buddhabhadra brought the Laṅkāvatāra and first opened the ordination platform at Faxing Monastery. Afterwards Master Zhiyao planted the bodhi tree beside the platform as a vanguard for the Sixth Patriarch. Several hundred years later Tripiṭaka Master Paramiti brought the Śūraṅgama Sutra, and when Minister Fang wrote it down at his dictation, Master Lu rose from among the woodcutter’s axes; and so the Buddhadharma began to flourish from Tang. Its root sprang up in Xinzhou, spread wide at Faxing, was dredged at Caoxi, and scattered through the realm. Thus we know that culture was gradually carried from China to the lands beyond the ridges, while the Chan Way was in fact carried from beyond the ridges into China. This is why they need each other and serve as a bridge for saving the world. Twelve years have passed since I crossed the ridges. Pitying the desolation of the Patriarch’s Way, I revived the family style of Caoxi; with this body of guilt and decay I met the edge of a hundred blows, and have fortunately come through unharmed these six years, relying on the protecting care of buddhas and patriarchs, and all things have their order. In the first days of establishing the Dharma way, those who drew near me in person at the assemblies were only Chaoyi and Tongjiong, two men. This shows how hard it is to teach and transform, and how hard beyond hard it is to gain men. Since Yi paid his respects to me, I have gone to Leiyang, walked the miasmic lands, and set Caoxi in order, hurrying to and fro with never a quiet day. Yi has respectfully followed the teaching, shut his door and swept his floor, and copied the great Avataṃsaka Sutra as his daily lesson; and with his remaining strength he sought out the old site of the Sixth Patriarch’s ordination platform, redeemed it, and rebuilt it. At leisure he led his fellows in forming a life-releasing society, with a fixed date each month, which gradually spread to the seacoast and was followed as a model — I indeed began it, but Yi and the rest were able to extend it. Now I have roughly completed the patriarchal seat and hope to rest in old age and finish my remaining years; and Yi follows me in roaming to the end of his life. Truly it is not only the beginning of rousing the mind that is hard, but even harder to bring it to completion. Yet what the ancients found hard, this man alone found easy: without good roots from many lives and a deep affinity with prajñā, how could it be so easy? Looking back at Shixing, a single breath failed and he was in everlasting kalpas; even to seek now that he might see and hear and rejoice in the various surpassing conditions before us — how could they be had again? So the rousing of the mind was the same but the former vows differed; hence their paths of birth and death diverged and they are forever parted in the darkness. We who have set our will on the great matter of birth and death may take warning from this. Yi and Xing asked instruction at the same time and copied this sutra; the words praising the Dharma stand at the head of the earlier section. For what Yi has copied I cannot add more words; I only set out thus how hard it is to rouse the mind and carry it through from first to last.
Colophon to the Avataṃsaka Sutra Copied by the Chan Monk Shixing

Our World-Honored One, Vairocana Tathāgata, when first he accomplished perfect awakening, in the bodhi site proclaimed the great Avataṃsaka, called the Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm, teaching the Dharma gate of the self-nature of beings as realized by all buddhas. Hence he said: ‘Wonderful, wonderful! All beings possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtuous marks, but because of deluded thinking, inversion, and attachment they do not realize them. If they leave deluded thinking and inversion, then all-wisdom, the wisdom without a teacher, appears of itself.’ Again he said: ‘I now, within the bodies of all beings, accomplish equal perfect awakening and turn the great Dharma wheel.’ Thus what this sutra expounds takes as its substance the one-flavored, equal great wisdom that perfectly illumines the Dharma realm, so that all saints and ordinary beings, their environments and bodies, the sentient and the insentient, are wholly equal; all the karmic actions of beings do not go beyond the self-nature Dharma body of the buddhas; all deluded thinking and ignorance, greed, hatred, delusion, and craving, are precisely the true suchness and true wisdom realized by the buddhas; and all mountains, rivers, and the great earth, all scale and shell, feather and fur, creeping and flying things, are precisely Vairocana’s universally manifested form body. So we know that in our daily use — turning and bowing, spitting and swinging the arms, even eating, drinking, rising, and resting — all is Samantabhadra’s wondrous practice and does not go beyond Vairocana Tathāgata’s ocean-seal samādhi. How much more for one who cultivates right practice and does pure works? It is only that we use it daily without knowing. Alas for men, deluded about this inherent wisdom, they drift on the stream of ignorance and karma, sink into birth and death, pass back and forth through the six paths, and endure every suffering — for how many hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds and dust-mote kalpas, they do not know. Never once do they turn back and reflect. Therefore our great Master, with equal great compassion, gave up the bliss of the self-nature Dharma and appeared in the world, thrusting himself into the three realms to open and guide them, entering deep into the burning house like an elder saving his children. Yet a father’s mind toward his son does not stop at merely sparing him calamity; he truly hopes to hand over the whole estate — this is his original heart. So at the very first he taught this sutra, suddenly revealing the equal Dharma realm and directly pointing to the self-nature Dharma body of beings, so that they might at once attain immeasurable Dharma bliss. Hence it is said: as in a single dust mote there is contained a great sutra scroll of a thousand worlds, written with the affairs of three thousand great thousand worlds, and a wise man sees it clearly within and breaks open the dust mote, brings out the sutra scroll, and holds it up for beings, turning it to their benefit. And the single dust mote is the deluded mind of beings; the great thousand-world sutra scroll is the self-nature merit of beings; the clear-eyed wise man is the great compassionate lord, the buddhas and bodhisattvas; breaking the dust mote is breaking the deluded thinking and inversion of men; and the means of breaking the dust mote is all the sutras and dharmas taught by the buddhas. Now the Dharma has sudden and gradual: the other sutras all break it gradually, while this Avataṃsaka is the sudden means, showing the vast treasury of Buddhadharma realized by the buddhas and wishing to let beings see it at a single glance and in a single thought at once obtain immeasurable enjoyment. From this we see that our Buddha’s grace and virtue toward beings are no shallow thing. Alas, since the Buddhadharma came into being this sutra has spread through the world, and many have seen and heard it; yet of those who can know the grace and virtue of the buddhas, how many are there? After our Buddha’s nirvāṇa, the patriarchs from of old who transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal and directly pointed to the Buddha-nature of beings were all true sons who could uphold the household of my compassionate father. It was for this matter especially that my Master Bodhidharma crossed the sea to this land, sat facing the wall at Shaolin in cold silence for nine years, and was poisoned four times, gaining only one man, the Second Patriarch, and then at once withdrawing west. Six generations brought it to my Master Dajian, who rose from among the woodcutter’s axes. Hearing one phrase of the sutra, he went at once to Huangmei, carried the pounding stone at his waist, and in the end obtained the robe and bowl and came south. Yet he was harmed by evil men more than once, and hid among the hunters for seventeen years; afterwards, when the conditions came, he borrowed a single phrase about wind and banner, shook gods and men, and was at last shaved and robed beneath the bodhi tree at Faxing, teaching the Dharma at the source of Caoxi. From this single line flowed seventeen hundred good teachers. All this vast merit and virtue came from a single thought of my Master’s patient endurance of suffering. Was he not a loyal minister of the Dharma king and a true son of the Tathāgata, the compassionate father? Even now the foundation of the ordination platform still stands, and the tree of the Way beneath which his hair was buried still remains. All beneath its shade rest at ease between heaven’s cover and earth’s support, eating the Master’s food and wearing the Master’s robe — yet of those who know the Master’s grace and think on the Master’s suffering there is not one. Alas, this may be called using it daily without knowing. I am humbly among the Master’s disciples of the Dharma-ending age. For spreading the Dharma I met with calamity and was banished to Leiyang. In bingshen I crossed the ridges and passed through Caoxi, and paid reverence to the Master, whose bodily remains were as solemn as if alive. Grieved that his Dharma way was desolate and its customs fallen, I wept several lines of tears for a long while. Then I went to my post. That autumn I returned to the walled camp at Qingmen in the provincial city. The next spring, deaths from famine and plague left white bones covering the fields, and those I gathered and buried numbered ten thousand. So I made a practice ground for ferrying and saving, and invited the assembled monks. The following year, wuxu, in the leisure between bearing the halberd, I led several disciples from beneath the tree and taught them the Dharma of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness. Then, having finished my commentary on the precious Laṅkāvatāra Sutra, I expounded it for them; and again I went beneath the tree and taught the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters to the novices, and the listeners grew daily more numerous. My disciples Chaoyi and Shixing took up incense and bowed, and said to me: ‘We wish to copy out the Avataṃsaka Sutra by hand, to serve as a bridge over the sea of suffering.’ I rejoiced and praised them. The two disciples shut their doors and burned incense, beginning in the gengzi year of Wanli; the following year, xinchou, Shixing suddenly passed away, having copied only twenty-seven fascicles. His master Chaozhen then ordered Shixing’s teacher Mingzhan to finish the work and complete this surpassing affinity. Alas, how sad! Beings wander in the bitter paths, passing through the six destinies like dust-mote kalpas and waves; among them, to meet the Buddhadharma and bring forth a faithful mind is like a one-eyed turtle in the great sea finding a hole in a floating log — how could it be easy? Now Shixing, born in this Dharma-ending age, relying on this surpassing cause, roams the heaven of the Flower Treasury without moving a step; at a single touch of the brush he beholds the ocean assembly of lands and dust motes, reveres Vairocana in the present moment, and perfects the ocean of practice through many kalpas. So his birth was not in vain and his death not wasted. How much more for one who rides this bridge and roams the land of no birth and no death! In the first month of winter in the renyin year I was about to set out for Leiyang, and Chaozhen brought the sutra Shixing had copied and begged a word from me to record the matter. I hope that those who later see and hear it may thereby bring forth a faithful mind; for if they can but turn the light around for a single thought, they will escape birth and death through vast kalpas. Then Shixing, from the tip of a single hair, again sends forth a broad and long tongue and teaches the Dharma gate of the self-nature of beings, no less than Vairocana seated at the bodhi tree — and this itself is the Dharma body abiding forever.
Colophon to the Avataṃsaka Sutra Copied by the Novices of Caoxi

How great is the sutra of the Dharma realm! Our original honored one, Rocana Buddha, when first he accomplished perfect awakening, sat in the forest grove at the bodhi site of Dharma, in the diamond mind-ground, and entered the ocean-seal samādhi, and according to his nature proclaimed the perfect and unobstructed, vast and majestic, freely attained Dharma gate: in seven places and nine assemblies, without rising he ascended and perfected the ten bodies. Stars spread through the Dharma realm; lands and dust motes, beings and their environments, all alike proclaim it, blazing without interval — an inconceivable Dharma. The Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi held the singly transmitted mind-seal; the robe and bowl from the West remain enshrined on this mountain. This very place is the bodhi site of Dharma, the diamond ground; his flesh body present before us is Rocana’s Dharma body abiding forever; the sound of bell and drum, morning and evening without interval, is the blazing teaching of lands and dust motes. Alas, his followers sit in the hall like the blind and deaf — face to face they have missed it for ages. In the past I received the sage’s compassion and was tamed across ten thousand miles, a grace too great to repay; and so I vowed to give up this body and set the practice ground in order again, seeking thereby to repay it. The disciples knew nothing of this matter at all, no different from the deaf and blind. So I selected young novices and taught them to practice writing, copying the honored Avataṃsaka Sutra, meaning to use this great Dharma affinity as a diamond seed. And indeed within a few years those who roused their minds to copy were ten in number. Master Ang, the hall master, was the teacher I had formerly engaged; he brought it to Mount Kuang. When I saw it I sighed: ‘This is the sutra brought out by breaking open a single dust mote. Looking at its dots and strokes, all flow from the diamond mind; how much more that the smallest novice vowed to prick his blood and copy it. This is what our Buddha called the wisdom without a teacher and the natural wisdom appearing before us.’ I was moved to tears, and regretted only that I could not be the novices’ ultimate guide. Yet even so, this is where my heart’s blood was sprinkled. If from now on those who see and hear rejoice, rouse their minds, and take it up, then affinity upon affinity without end, down to the future limit, will lead the disciples of Caoxi each to enter this Dharma gate — so that dust preaches, lands preach, beings preach, and this Dharma is turned blazingly forever. Then Rocana teaches in the present, the Sixth Patriarch abides here forever, and though I die I shall not perish. How can I contain my joy! Respectfully I write the original causes and conditions, to show those who come, to serve as a ground for rousing the mind, and to be the old man’s broad and long tongue.
Colophon to the Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows Written in Blood by a Caoxi Novice

When I formerly dwelt at Caoxi and restored the Patriarch’s Way, I trained the novices in the hope that the work that came from the West would not be lost. In less than ten years there seemed to be a change. Among the community one novice roused his mind to prick his blood and copy the Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows, to recite and uphold all his life. The old man sighed deeply and said: ‘This novice knows the Dharma, that he can prick his blood and copy this sutra, performing this difficult and great work. The dependent arising of the Dharma realm knows no distinction of deluded and awakened, belongs to neither sage nor ordinary; whatever is done with greatness returns to the ultimate. It is said that mountains, rivers, and the great earth all turn the root Dharma wheel, and scale, shell, feather, and fur all manifest the samādhi of the form body. How much more this blood of the body, flowing from the Dharma realm and dripping into this sutra — is it not one with true Dharma-nature? If the novice copies thus and recites thus, unwearied to the end of his life, then thought after thought he does not leave Samantabhadra’s ocean of practice, and step by step he does not leave the practice ground of the Flower Treasury. Only believe without doubt: beyond this there is no other Buddhadharma. Thus the old man’s praise, though measured to the Dharma realm, could not exhaust the full measure of that merit. But if one is blind to one’s own mind and every movement goes against the Dharma, then though one see the King of Vows face to face, one only adds to the consciousness of karma.’
The Pure Rules of the Permanent Community
The Master entered the mountain and arrived at the monastery on the twentieth day of the ninth month of the twenty-eighth year.

From the seventh day of the tenth month to the ninth day, for three days, in the hall he carefully selected monks and novices of the whole monastery, great and small, to recite sutras and study. On the ninth day the Lotus Hall was established. At the hour of the hare the bell was struck three times, and all assembled in the Buddha hall; the arrangement was not to be delayed, and robes had to be worn neatly, each bringing a copy of the Lotus Sutra, or two sharing one if need be, all complete at the same time without omission or error. On the thirteenth day three schools of instruction were established. The east cloister school opened at the hour of the horse on the thirteenth day of the tenth month.
The west cloister school opened at the hour of the tiger on the thirteenth day of the tenth month.
The Yanshou school opened at the hour of the serpent on the thirteenth day of the tenth month.
The Pure Rules of the Ten-Direction Permanent Community of the Baolin Chan Hall at Caoxi

Our Sixth Patriarch taught the Dharma at Caoxi, and the wandering monks of the world gathered to him. The Patriarch established a settled community to accommodate the great assembly: this was the first beginning of the founding of a Chan hall. Then Master Baizhang established rules and regulations to govern a multitude: this was the first institution of pure rules. From that time every monastery in the world has had a Chan hall and practiced pure rules, and has been called a ten-direction permanent community, so that though its fingers number ten million, it is as one body, head, eyes, hands, and feet mutually dependent.
But the Caoxi Chan hall, since the Sixth Patriarch, is now a thousand years old; in time it fell into disuse. The monks of this monastery dispersed their fires and scattered, dwelling in different places, and the pure rules were not practiced, so that even the wandering monks of the ten directions who came to pay reverence to the Patriarch were utterly without refuge. Though the patriarchal seat stood, there was no longer the work of pure practice; at the worst it was no different from the common people. How could this be the root ground of the Chan source? The old man, by the sage’s grace, crossed the ridges; receiving the abundant goodwill of the protectors of the Dharma in office, and unable to bear the decline of the patriarchal seat, they commanded the monastery’s monks to invite me to set it in order. On arriving I bent my whole mind to one purpose, taking the restoration of the Patriarch’s Way as my heart. Besides repairing the halls, I cleared the old site of Baolin: the monks’ quarters were crowded together, so I donated funds to buy vacant land elsewhere and moved seven monks’ quarters, opening out one whole section. I again established an inner Chan hall to house the permanent community, and an outer hall to receive the comings and goings of the ten directions. Beyond the incense and lamps of the permanent community, I donated my own funds to redeem the fields of the Zisun estate, its mountain gardens and lands, as support; this is called the ten-direction permanent community.
Now that the dwelling is settled and the four requisites complete, I fear that those who dwell in this hall may not discipline themselves and advance in the Way, and that the one in charge of the hall, if unacquainted with the pure rules of the ancient worthies, may err in affairs and deviate in word and deed, harming the Dharma gate — thus wronging not only the heart of the founding but truly betraying the protectors, dragons, and gods. So for daily affairs I set out a few regulations as below; host and guest alike should observe them, to seek the lasting glorification of the Patriarch’s Way. Thus may the Dharma gate not fall and the work of the Way be accomplished. The old man, looking up to continue the threadlike line of the Sixth Patriarch, thereby somewhat expresses his original vow. All my disciples must keep them; be careful not to neglect them.
The Buddha said there are two kinds of permanent community. The first is the permanent community proper, that is, the present monastery, which appoints an abbot to preside, called the elder, the leader of the whole monastery. The second is the ten-direction permanent community, that is, the present Chan hall, which appoints a hall master to preside, the leader of the ten directions. Hence those who dwell in this hall, whether inner or outer, are all called ten-direction, because they have roused the mind to practice and their resolve transcends the world, unlike worldly men.
As for the pure rules of ritual, they follow the pattern of the abbot; but between the abbot and the monks there is a distinction of high and low. One who presides over the Chan hall with Dharma and food held equal has the relation of teacher and student and is called hall head, as at Shaolin today. One who merely manages the affairs of the Chan hall is called hall master and stands in the relation of host and guest with the community, as in the various places today. All the monks in the hall depend in truth on the four requisite conditions for daily aid in the Way; all affairs of the monastery, great and small, rely on him to bear them, while the community merely folds its hands. This is no small matter. So there must be mutual respect, harmony within and without, and the Way held in heart; do not recklessly give rise to discussion or seek out faults. The ritual and pure rules of this place have their fixed pattern: keep your station and hold to what is established, and do not recklessly add or subtract.
The founding of a Chan hall is no light thing, and the office of hall master is very heavy, for the eyes of the ten directions are fixed on one man. His words and deeds must be upright and pure, to answer the community’s hopes. Hence one who holds this office must embrace a compassionate mind, a broad mind, a gentle mind, a patient mind, a humble mind — the mind of a bodhisattva’s practice, like a bridge, like the great earth — and only then can he bear beings and be called one of wondrous practice. So in daily food and drink he shares sweet and bitter with the community and must not secretly favor any; a drop of water or a stalk of vegetables he holds with the community at heart, and must not follow his own will alone and invite ridicule. When monks do wrong, he should inform the chief seats and settle it with gentle words and skillful means; he must not suddenly break out in violent and coarse speech, scolding as his feelings dictate. He must not be harsh to the tenant farmers and so draw resentment. In all appointments he must weigh whether the man is worthy and must not recklessly use the wrong person.
As for the money and grain of the permanent community, he should restrain extravagant spending and not overspend; what must be spent should first be discussed with the chief seats, the records examined and the expenditure clearly entered, and he must not act on his own will alone. The hall’s annual budget rests on the permanent community’s rents, which fall short by a third every year; the deficit is very great, and there is no reliable source, so we rely only on the community’s practice to move the dragons, gods, and outer protectors. All of it rests on the hall master’s single shoulder to beg and transform. Should it still fall short, the community should only share the same plain fare and not seek abundance, nor recklessly borrow debts to burden the permanent community. The working monks labor with bitter hearts and strength all year in hardship; in the two seasons of winter and summer they must be given cloth in due measure to aid their hearts in the Way. But as the permanent community’s annual budget falls short, it is truly hard to fix a rule; it lies with the hall master to devise ways in many directions; otherwise the working monks cannot be at peace.
The resident monks of the hall should in principle be equal; but where strength does not reach, it is hard to manage. Borrowing would burden the permanent community and could not last. If it is done at the eighth-month assembly, the conditions are hard to fix; and if anything is borrowed in advance, it must be repaid at once. Now, according to whatever offerings come in, first repay what is owed, and distribute the rest to the hall in due measure according to amount, to aid the conditions of the Way — a fixed rule being difficult. If there is more, store it to fill out the permanent community, so that it is not left empty, and thus it may last. Should a donor give with single purpose, let it follow his own intention, not belonging to the usual rule.
The hall’s annual budget rests entirely on the eighth-month assembly, when donors gather. Of the offerings for feeding monks, rice goes into the granary; as for silver, a chest and a ledger should be set up, and the secretary should ask one upright man to keep them jointly. Silver received in place of rice must be entered in the ledger truthfully and in the presence of witnesses; it must not be converted to other use or secretly embezzled. Silver for providing the vegetarian feasts must likewise be entered and stored in the ledger, and spent day by day before the assembly; the secretary shall keep a separate ledger of expenditure for audit. The hall master may not take in or pay out privately. Silver for chanting sutras and bowing in repentance must likewise be entered in the ledger, to be distributed to the community at the close of the assembly; the hall may not hold it as its own, for within and without the practice ground there is one strength, and so it may not be monopolized. If tea and fruit are sent from outside for the hall master, he may take them for himself; what is sent for the hall, and for such occasions as notice-boards, memorials, and Buddhist services, belongs to those in charge in the hall; if the donor’s intention is fixed on them, they may take them openly. Those who transgress the rule and contend for them shall, according to the pure rules, be fined several times the amount contended for; and those who will not obey in providing a vegetarian feast shall not dwell together.
The monks sitting in the hall are all under training. The monks of this monastery live nearby, close to relatives and friends; but I fear old haunts are hard to forget, so they must not repeatedly find pretexts to return to their rooms, give free rein to drinking and gambling, wander and play, or come to the hall drunk, offending the spirits and slighting the rules of ritual. Those who offend: the hall master shall inform the chief seats; the grave shall not dwell together, the light shall be punished before the community by kneeling with a stick of incense, repenting and reforming. Those who do not obey shall also not dwell together.
The monks in the hall are all trained by the old man to glorify the Patriarch’s Way; let them take practice alone as their heart. Each should carefully keep the precepts, discipline the three karmas, subdue offenses, and not create karma. They must not gather their heads to raise reckless discussion, delude upright men, and start trouble; nor lead in lawless men to destroy the permanent community or steal its goods. Whoever violates this shall be punished with the offender. All affairs of the hall and its annual expenditure rest on the hall master’s single strength; for one man to shoulder the affairs of many, it is truly hard to have everything exactly right. If there is a fault, the community should also be understanding and remember his toil, and must not demand perfection and blame him, recklessly pointing out faults and giving rise to other talk. If there is indeed a fault, they should join with the chief seats in the abbot’s quarters over tea, speaking frankly and remonstrating rightly; they must not suddenly utter coarse words and wound the body of the Way.
All wandering monks who come from afar in the ten directions rest in the pilgrims’ lodge of the outer hall. They must enter the hall and exchange greetings; the chief seats should at once lead the community in returning the courtesy and expressing thanks, and the guest master should offer tea, not sitting in rudeness and so offending the ten directions. If it is a teacher of Dharma or a worthy monk of high virtue, they should inform the hall master, who should invite him into the inner hall’s guest room to dwell, whether for a winter or a summer, and must do his utmost to serve and make offerings with reverence; the community should consult him morning and evening on the essentials of the Dharma and must not be disrespectful and so add to their offenses. Those who rest three or five days in the pilgrims’ lodge shall have their meals from the inner store; the hall master must constantly keep it in mind and inspect it, not letting there be lack, and should appoint a lodge master to manage reception. If a feast is provided in the inner hall, the next hall should also be called upon. The affairs of the Chan hall are extremely simple: the rents are merely collected by the chief seats, or the hall master may collect them himself, so there is no need to establish many officers. But one guest master is indispensable, to answer comings and goings and receive the wandering monks of the ten directions. This office lies in getting the right man; if the man is lacking, a monk on daily duty in the hall may manage it in his place. When a guest arrives he must be detained and served tea; if a donor comes with single purpose, the hall master must be informed and received with courtesy, and his faith must not be turned back. As for wandering monks, one must distinguish the worthy from the foolish and not lightly keep or dismiss them.
In the public affairs of the monastery, nothing is divided into inner and outer: all alike are called upon. This is the common rule of the world, ancient and modern. In this mountain, the provisions for the Way come from the donors’ own feasts, the estate rents are delivered by the tenants themselves, and firewood is gathered by the working monks going into the mountain; beyond this there is not much labor. Only carrying firewood from the stream and tending the vegetables in the garden. When a general call comes to the hall, only one man on daily duty stays to watch the hall, and all the rest go together; none may evade, and offenders are punished by kneeling with a stick of incense.
In the monasteries of the world, whether inner or outer, the Dharma family is of one body. Those in the hall rely on the working monks to aid their work of the Way, and the working monks give their strength to support practice; in truth the laborers are the greater number, and only one whose mind in the Way is firm can long relish bitter practice. They are largely not to be compared with worldly servants. In all public affairs of the permanent community, when the chief seats of the Chan hall lead the community and direct the work, all must obey and none may resist. As for each man’s private affairs, unless there is close friendship, they may not be commanded privately. If among the working monks below there is crowding and clamor, or waste of food, or favoritism in food and drink, or any of various offenses, the cook is first to discipline them; if they are not harmonious, the hall master decides, with dismissal or retention settled by reason according to the pure rules. If the hall sees an offense, it should also inform the hall master to deal with it, and must not of itself utter coarse words and insults, giving rise to contention. Whether a working monk is acceptable, the hall master understands the whole situation and it cannot be judged from one side alone. The estate tenants may not be used without public business; the settling of working monks below rests wholly on the hall master’s inspection; none may out of private feeling keep relatives and friends by force, lest there be lawlessness that destroys the permanent community and brings trouble on the one who recommended them; if the matter comes out, the offender and his sponsor are punished alike.
Those in the hall are all monks of this monastery under training. Now that the monastery has order and its scale is impressive, there may be men of the younger generation of this monastery, of no virtue by nature, who will not accept the instruction of their teacher, who covet idleness and ease, and who use entering the hall as a pretext: they must on no account be admitted. Or having entered the hall, they do not keep the pure rules and precepts, give free rein to wild conduct, do not join the community in recitation, devote themselves to laziness, or are often outside drinking wine and eating meat, utterly without shame, trusting only to empty reputation and not attending to true practice, stirring up the group and disrupting the community: the chief seats and rejoicing officers of the hall shall ask the hall master to inform the abbot and the heads together, and they shall be expelled from the hall at once, not permitted to remain long and injure the community’s virtue. Those who do not obey shall be dealt with by the abbot according to the rule; be careful not to yield to private feeling and breed future harm.
The monasteries of the world have the Pure Rules of Baizhang, forever a settled law. But this mountain’s Chan hall, though named ten-direction, is not to be compared with other places. When the old man entered the mountain, he earnestly reflected that the Patriarch’s Way had declined and the monks had lost their proper calling; the old man’s will was set on restoration, taking men of talent as the root. So at first he donated the fees he received to teach the novices; when they were shaved he built the Chan hall to teach them practice, and donated his robe funds to establish support — every kind of bitter effort in training them, all of it on high for the Sixth Patriarch, to continue the vein of the Way, and below to receive the ten directions, to glorify the monastery. Now, alas, the old man’s virtue is thin and he could not fulfill his original vow; he abandoned it midway and left. So a ten-direction hall master is appointed to take the old man’s place in his toil. But all that is needed is still much lacking, and though the hall master embodies the old man’s heart and vow, he does not have the old man’s power of the Way; I fear there will be omissions and he cannot cover everything. The heads, officers, and elders of this monastery should all be understanding, and reflect that the patriarchal seat without a Chan hall is not worthy of the name of a practice ground, and without a hall master cannot receive the ten directions and keep a large community; and if it belonged to this monastery alone, it would inevitably yield to worldly custom and soon fall into disuse. Therefore this mountain and the hall master stand in the relation of host and guest; each should hold the Way in heart, and host and guest should each fulfill their courtesies, not recklessly blaming and demanding, wounding harmony, ruining the monastery, betraying the old man’s intention in building it, incurring guilt before the Sixth Patriarch, and drawing the censure of dragons and gods. This should be carefully guarded against.

The regulations above are many, and I cannot set them all out. Even what is listed here, though not the ancient rule, is meant to save the ills of the times. In this Baolin practice ground, if each can be followed and practiced, then the revival of the Patriarch’s Way lies in this endeavor. Pray do not regard them as commonplace and lightly neglect them, betraying the heart of the founding. Let all in the hall strive to keep them.
On the twelfth day of the eleventh month of the forty-first year of Wanli, the Elder Hanshan, Deqing, of the restored Baolin Chan Hall at Caoxi, wrote this at the ten-direction permanent community.

blocks.text: Preface to Master Hanshan’s Record of the Restoration of Caoxi

inline.s: In the gengzi year I was stationed with troops at Nan-Shao. Reflecting that Caoxi had sunk into the Dharma-ending age and that the Buddha’s realm had nearly become a marketplace, I drove out all the butchers and wine-sellers and the idlers, along with the pigs, ducks, and geese they kept, and enjoined the monks to cut off wine and meat forever; even when guests came they drank only tea or ate a vegetarian meal, so that it might deserve to be called a pure practice ground, and that the flesh-body Bodhisattva might not be troubled with kalpa after kalpa of Avīci karma. The monks were at first fearful, then praised and rejoiced, as though escaping boiling water and being bathed in cool water. The words are all in my Guangdong Travels. At that time Master Hanshan was teaching the Dharma at Wuyang, and monks and laymen far and near looked up to him as a dragon or elephant. I was about to go to court to congratulate the emperor on his long life, and on departing I feared the monks’ habitual karma would be hard to wash away and that in the Dharma-ending age it would end in oblivion; so I asked the Master to come and preside over this mountain. I questioned him face to face at Wuyang, saying that this single tract of Baolin was a great matter of affinity for a thousand ages, and that unless the Master took it on his shoulders, who would? The Master assented. He escorted me as far as Lingzhou and there we parted. Now it is the xinyou year, and I have again come to Guangdong on a mission concerning the sea; passing Baolin, more than twenty years have slipped by — truly a mere bending and stretching of the arm — and it is some eight years since the Master left Baolin. Seeing what he rebuilt, its orderly arrangements grave and solemn, and the monks all docile, robed and chanting, compared with the past when they wore loincloths and carried hoes, stuffed and drunk, unable to read a single character — they seem like men who have changed their very bones, three lifetimes removed. Their longing for the Master and hope of his return at any moment is nothing less than an infant’s longing for its mother. They therefore begged a few lines from me and went to Mount Kuang to press the Master. Before long I received the imperial grace recalling me to the auxiliary capital. My boat returned by Qingxi, still three stages short of Caoxi, and the monks came with a letter from the Master and the Caoxi Record he had compiled. Opening it, the first thing he put to me was the words about dream, illusion, bubbles, and shadow, deeply moved by the impermanence of the world’s partings and meetings, comings and goings. And reading through the Record, everything in it is conditioned dharma. Now if, as he says, all is within deluded thought and all is illusion, then Baolin and Caoxi are illusion too, and the monasteries, the bodily remains, the robe and bowl — none but illusion. Why then trouble the monks with these dense regulations and the minutiae of rice and salt? And does not the Record take the rule of the permanent community as a law for the monks? All conditioned things are the dharma of abiding; but what he calls dream, illusion, bubbles, and shadow is the dharma of non-abiding. Only with the abiding can there be non-abiding; only with non-abiding can there be abiding and constant non-abiding; only with abiding and constant non-abiding can there be neither abiding nor non-abiding. Only by abiding do dreams, illusions, and emptiness not obstruct existence; only by constant non-abiding do all dharmas and existence not obstruct emptiness. If the monks proceed from not daring to slight the Dharma to not clinging to the Dharma, then in the Record the Master compiled, the dreams he speaks of, and the comings and goings, partings and meetings, emptiness and existence he feels — all mutually contain without obstructing one another. This is the original purport of buddhas and patriarchs, and the inexhaustible purport of the ancient worthies. I shall dwell a few kalpas with the Master in dream, illusion, bubble, and shadow, and discuss it further; let the Master send me a turning phrase in reply. Written in the first month of autumn in the renxu year of Tianqi by Zhu Yiyou of western Zhejiang, Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments at Nanjing.
The Dream-Journey Collection of Elder Hanshan, Volume Fifty-Three

blocks.text: The Elder Hanshan’s Autobiographical Chronicle, Part One

inline.s: The twenty-fifth year of Jiajing, bingwu.

My family name was Cai. My father was Yangao; my mother, of the Hong family, loved all her life to serve the Bodhisattva Guanyin. At first she dreamed that the Bodhisattva led a boy through the door, and she received and embraced him, and so conceived. At birth I was wrapped in a double caul as white as cloth. I was born in the jichou hour of the twelfth day, being the bingshen day, of the tenth month, jihai, of that year.
The twenty-sixth year, dingwei.

At one year old I was seized with a wind illness and nearly died. My mother prayed to the Bodhisattva and vowed to give me up to leave home, and had my name enrolled at the Changshou Monastery of the county; my milk name was accordingly changed to Heshang, ‘the monk.’
The twenty-seventh year, wushen.
At three I often sat alone, not caring to play with other children. My grandfather used to say, ‘This child is like a wooden post.’
The twenty-eighth year, jiyou.
The twenty-ninth year, gengxu.
The thirtieth year, xinhai.
The thirty-first year, renzi.

At seven I was dearly loved by my uncle. My parents sent me to the village school. One day my uncle died and lay on the bed. When I came home my mother deceived me, saying, ‘Your uncle is asleep; call him to get up.’ I called several times, and my aunt, pierced with grief, wept and cried, ‘O Heaven, where has he gone?’ I was astonished and doubted. I asked my mother, ‘Uncle’s body is here — where else has he gone?’ My mother said, ‘Your uncle is dead.’ I said, ‘Where do the dead go?’ And I doubted this keenly. Before long my second aunt gave birth to a son. My mother went to look, and I followed. Seeing the infant so large, I asked my mother, ‘How did this child get into aunt’s belly?’ My mother slapped me and said, ‘Silly boy, how did you get into your mother’s belly?’ And again I doubted keenly. From this the doubt about where the dead go and where the living come from could not be resolved in my breast.
The thirty-second year, guichou.

At eight I studied and boarded with relatives across the river. My mother warned me not to come home, but to return only once a month. One day I came home and, clinging to my mother, would not go back. She was angry and whipped me, driving me to the riverside. I would not get into the boat; in her anger she seized me by the topknot and threw me into the river, and without a backward look went home. My grandmother saw it and called out in haste, and I was pulled out and taken home. My mother said, ‘This worthless child — why keep him if he is not drowned?’ And she beat me and drove me out again, showing no attachment at all. At that time I privately thought my mother hard-hearted, and from then on I did not think of home. My mother often wept across the river; my grandmother scolded her, and she said, ‘I must cut off his affection, for only so can he study.’
The thirty-third year, jiayin.

At nine I studied in a monastery and heard the monks chant the Guanyin Sutra, which can save the world from suffering. My heart rejoiced greatly. I asked a monk for the text, read it in secret, and could soon recite it. My mother served the Bodhisattva Guanyin and burned incense and bowed each time, and I always followed her. One day I said to my mother, ‘The Bodhisattva Guanyin has a sutra.’ She said, ‘I did not know.’ I at once recited it through for her. My mother was overjoyed and said, ‘Where did you get this? Even the sound of your chanting is like an old monk’s.’
The thirty-fourth year, yimao.

At ten my mother supervised my lessons very strictly, and I suffered under it. So I asked my mother, ‘What is study for?’ She said, ‘To be an official.’ I asked, ‘What kind of official?’ She said, ‘You begin small; at best you can reach prime minister.’ I said, ‘And when one has been prime minister, what then?’ She said, ‘Then it ends.’ I said, ‘A whole life of hardship, and in the end it ends. What use is it? I think one should be something that does not end.’ My mother said, ‘A worthless child like you could only be a wandering monk.’ I asked, ‘What is a wandering monk? What good is that?’ She said, ‘A monk is a disciple of the Buddha. He travels the whole world, free and at ease, and is supported wherever he goes.’ I said, ‘That is exactly the thing to be.’ My mother said, ‘I fear only that you have not the blessing for it.’ I asked, ‘Why does it need blessing?’ She said, ‘A man who takes first place in the imperial examination is common enough in the world; but one who leaves home and becomes a buddha or patriarch — how often does that happen?’ I said, ‘I have that blessing; I fear only that my mother cannot give me up.’ She said, ‘If you have that blessing, I can give you up.’ I secretly noted this in my heart.
The thirty-fifth year, bingchen.

At eleven I happened to see several wandering monks coming with their gourds and bamboo hats on carrying poles. I asked my mother who they were. She said, ‘Wandering monks.’ I was secretly delighted and watched them. When the monks arrived they set down their poles and leaned against a tree, then greeted us and asked for a meal. My mother said, ‘Please sit,’ and quickly boiled tea and prepared a vegetarian meal with great reverence. When they had eaten, the monks rose, took up their poles, and merely raised a hand. My mother quickly stepped aside, saying, ‘Do not thank me.’ The monks went straight off. I said, ‘How rude these monks are, not thanking us for the meal.’ My mother said, ‘To thank would be to lose the blessing.’ I said privately, ‘This is what makes a monk lofty.’ I thought of it earnestly, and so brought forth the resolve to leave home, though I bitterly lacked the means.
The thirty-sixth year, dingyi.

At twelve I studied and understood the meaning of texts, and the villagers and my clan all loved and respected me. I was never happy with worldly life. My father arranged a marriage for me, and I stopped it at once. One day I heard a monk from the capital say that the Great Monk Xilin of Bao’en Monastery was a man of great virtue, and my heart wished at once to go and follow him. I told my father, who would not hear of it; I told my mother, who said, ‘In raising a son one follows his resolve; only let him succeed.’ So she sent me. In the tenth month of that year I reached the monastery. The Grand Master Elder saw me and said with joy at once, ‘This child’s bone-spirit is uncommon; if he becomes an ordinary monk, it will be a pity. I will merely engage a teacher to instruct him in study and see how he turns out.’ At that time Great Master Wuji had just begun lecturing in the monastery’s Tripiṭaka Hall, and my grand-master took me to pay respects. Lord Zhao Dazhou happened to be there, and seeing me he said with joy at once, ‘This child will be a teacher of gods and men.’ He stroked me and asked, ‘Do you wish to be an official, or to become a buddha?’ I answered on the instant, ‘To become a buddha.’ Lord Zhao said, ‘This child must not be made light of; he should be well taught.’ When I heard the lecture, though I did not know what was being said, my heart churned as though I knew something and could not express it. At that time Brother Xuelang En was one year older than I and had left home under the Master a year earlier; seeing me, he looked at me and smiled, and people took us for brothers. In Jiangnan the lecturing of Buddhadharma began with Great Master Wuji; and of youths who entered the Buddhadharma, the first was Xuelang.
The thirty-seventh year, wuwu.

At thirteen, my grand-master ancestor first chose from among his descendants one of learning and practice, Master Jun, to be my teacher. He first taught me the Lotus Sutra, which I could recite through in four months.
The thirty-eighth year, jiwei.

At fourteen I could recite all the sutras then in circulation. The Grand Master Elder said, ‘This child can be taught and must not be misdirected.’ So he engaged a teacher skilled in letters to instruct me.
The thirty-ninth year, gengshen.

At fifteen the Grand Master Elder engaged a tutor to teach me the examination curriculum. He first tested whether I could be taught, and then had me read the Four Books straight through. That year I was often ill.
The fortieth year, xinyou.
At sixteen I finished the Four Books that year and recited them from memory, not missing a single character from beginning to end.
The forty-first year, renxu.

At seventeen I studied the Four Books that year, read the Book of Changes, and also practiced examination essays and ancient prose, verse, and rhapsody. I could already compose poems and write prose, and among the youths of the time none was reckoned my superior.
The forty-second year, guihai.

At eighteen, the education commissioner of the time lectured exclusively on the Learning of the Way and used the young candidates as singing boys, dozens of them following him about and singing in file, and some even advanced to office through this. I was deeply ashamed of it and wished to abandon my studies. That year, on account of illness, I declined and did not enter the school.
The forty-third year, jiazi.

At nineteen, all my friends in the same association passed the examinations, and some urged me to go and sit for them. At that time Great Master Yungu, a true eye of the Dharma, was dwelling in Qixia Mountain. The Grand Master Elder had long supported him, and whenever he came or went he would be kept and entertained for ten days or a month. I attended him very diligently. When Great Master Yun came out from the mountain and heard that others had urged me, he feared I might be of a mind to leave; so with all his strength he instructed me in the wonder of leaving the world, inquiring into Chan, and awakening clearly to the mind-ground. He recounted the patriarchs of the lamp transmission and the biographies of eminent monks one by one, and had me fetch and read them. Searching my book chest, I found the Extensive Record of Zhongfeng. Before I had finished a single scroll I was filled with joy, and sighed: ‘This is what my heart delights in.’ So I resolved to undertake the matter of leaving the world. I at once asked the Grand Elder to shave me, burned and cast away all I had studied, and set my mind solely on investigating the one matter. Not yet having its essentials, I devoted myself to reciting the Buddha’s name day and night without interruption. Before long, one night in a dream I saw Amitābha Buddha appear standing in the air at the place where the sun sets, and beheld his face and eye-light, his marks, clear and distinct. I bowed at his feet in reverence, and my grieving longing would not cease. I then wished to see the two bodhisattvas Guanyin and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and they at once appeared half-bodied. From that time the three holy ones were ever blazing before my eyes, and I believed that practice could be accomplished. In the winter of that year the monastery’s Chan hall held a practice session and invited Great Master Wuji to lecture on the Profound Discourse on the Avataṃsaka. I received the full precepts and followed the lecture as far as the ten profound gates, ‘the ocean-seal wherein all things are arrayed in their constante abode,’ when I suddenly awakened and understood the purport of the Dharma realm’s perfect fusion without end. I deeply admired the life of Qingliang, and so named myself Chengyin, ‘Clear Seal,’ and asked the Master to confirm it. The Master said, ‘Is your will set on entering this Dharma gate?’ And because he had seen the words that Mount Qingliang has hard ice piled in winter and still flying snow in summer, and never any scorching heat, and is therefore called Qingliang, ‘Clear and Cool,’ from that time the realm of ice and snow was ever present before me as I walked and stood, and I vowed to dwell in it. Nothing in any affair could please my mind, and the thought of leaving the world never left me for a moment.
The forty-fourth year, yichou.

At twenty, on the sixteenth day of the first month of that year, the Grand Master Elder entered quiescence. On the last day of the previous year he had gathered all his kin and said, ‘I am eighty-three; my going is a matter of dawn or dusk. I have saved more than eighty disciples, and not one upholds my work.’ Then, stroking my back, he said, ‘This child I hoped would grow to manhood; now I cannot wait for it. Though he is young, he has the views of an elder. After my death, all affairs of the household, great and small, shall be decided by him; do not make light of him because he is small.’ The assembly, sobbing, accepted the charge. On the seventh day of the new year the Elder, robed, went around the quarters bidding each farewell, and all were astonished. Three days later he arranged his after-affairs, showed a slight illness, and refused to take medicine, saying, ‘I am going; what use is medicine?’ He then gathered the community to recite the Buddha’s name for five days and nights, holding his prayer beads; I held him in my arms, and he passed away upright and serene, because all his life he had upheld the Diamond Sutra and did not cease even at the end. The Grand Master Elder had been the official incumbent of Bao’en for thirty years and dwelt in the abbot’s quarters; and on the eighteenth day of the third month after his entry into quiescence the abbot’s quarters burned down, and all marveled at it. In the tenth month of that winter Great Master Yungu established a Chan session at Tiantai, gathering fifty-three men of renown and virtue from within the seas to open the Dharma gate of sitting meditation. The Master pressed me hard to go with him, and the junior Master Elder allowed it, and so I was able to join the session. At first I did not know the secret of applying the mind and suffered greatly. So I took up incense and asked instruction, and the Master revealed to me the huatou of Buddha-recitation, to be investigated until it is verified. From then on I inquired into it without a single thought shifting. Within three months I was as if in a dream, seeing no assembly at all and not knowing there were daily affairs; and everyone took me for a man of resolve. Yet within the first few days, because I applied my mind too urgently, a carbuncle suddenly broke out on my back, red, swollen, and huge, and the Master was greatly troubled by it. Wearing my robe, I prayed with bitter earnestness before Weituo: ‘This must be karmic debt demanding my life. I vow to recite the Avataṃsaka Sutra ten times and ask leave of absence for three months to finish the Chan session, afterwards repaying it.’ In the latter part of the night, utterly exhausted, I climbed onto the meditation bed and fell fast asleep, not even hearing the signal to rise; and when I got up I had forgotten all about it. At dawn the Master asked how my ailment was. I said, ‘It is nothing.’ And when he looked, it had quite healed. The whole assembly marveled. So I was able to complete the session. When I came out, I was as though I had never left the meditation seat: even walking in the marketplace, I seemed to see no one, and all thought it strange. Jiangnan had never known Chan, and the founding of the Chan way began with Great Master Yungu. Of young monks practicing Chan I was the only one. At that time the monks’ dress all followed worldly fashion and was much given to bright colors; I cast off all the clothes I had and sought out a single patched robe to cover myself, and those who saw it thought it strange.
The forty-fifth year, bingyin.

At twenty-one, having come out from the Chan session, at noon on the eighteenth day of the second month of that year, rain fell like a downpour, and suddenly a great thunderbolt came down from the pagoda and fire broke out in the pagoda hall. In no time the great hall was burned; and by the hours of shen and you all the halls and galleries, more than one hundred and forty bays, were reduced to ashes. At that time my junior grand-master was abbot, and when the matter was reported to the throne an edict went down to the judicial office, and eighteen men who had been involved were arrested. The monks of the whole monastery, fearing they would be implicated, all fled, and among the officers of the monastery there was no one with whom to plan. I thrust myself forward to save them, carrying salt and vegetables on my own back twenty li to the ministry of justice to supply them, going and coming untiring for three months and sheltering them in many ways, so that all involved escaped death. At that time Brother Xuelang En and I both resolved to restore the monastery, saying: ‘This great matter of affinity is not easy for one who lacks great merit, virtue, and wisdom. You and I should stake our lives on practice and wait for the time.’ It was then that I formed the resolve to travel far. Soon after, my junior grand-master entered quiescence, and there was no one to support the household of the Grand Ancestor. Earlier, when the Grand Master Elder entered quiescence, there were no savings, and the funeral expenses were all met by borrowing without limit, so there were many debts. When the household was divided, I knew it could not be preserved. Mindful of the Grand Master Elder’s dying charge, I found means to repay all the debts, and divided the remainder among the disciples so that each might take up a livelihood, and the household was preserved. In the winter of that year I followed Great Master Wuji and heard the Lotus Sutra at Tiantai Monastery. Because I had resolved on distant travel, I kept observing the monks of the various quarters, seeking one who could be my companion; for a long time I found none. One day I saw the rear latrine swept clean and thought that the latrine keeper must be no ordinary man, so I sought him out. When I saw him he was only a monk sick with yellow edema, yet every morning before dawn his work was all done, and I never knew when he swept. So I stayed awake and secretly paced the corridor to watch: while the community was still at rest, he had already finished. A few days later I found it unclean and the man gone. I asked, and the officer said, ‘The latrine keeper is sick in the guest quarters.’ I went to look, and his condition was pitiable. I asked, ‘Is the Master well?’ He said, ‘This karmic body’s illness is already hard to bear; the illness of craving is harder still.’ I asked why. He said, ‘Whenever I see the food being distributed, I hate that I cannot swallow it all at once.’ I laughed and said, ‘That is only hunger from long illness.’ And I knew the man was genuine. So I prepared cakes and fruit, carried them in my sleeve, and went to see him, asking his name: Miaofeng, a man of Puzhou. I at once made a pact with him to travel together. A few days later I went again, and he was gone. In my heart I knew the man, and feared he had gone quietly lest he be a burden to me.
The first year of Longqing, dingmao.

At twenty-two I especially proposed Master Xugu Zhong as abbot of the monastery, to save it from ruin. Because of the fire, the permanent community owed nearly a thousand taels, all of it having passed through my hands. The community could think of no way to deal with it. I devised a plan and set a limit of three years to repay it all. That year, by a ministry directive, the monastery established a school of instruction to teach monks; I was asked to be the teacher, and I taught more than one hundred and fifty novices. Because of this I again looked at the Zuo Commentary and the ancient prose of the philosophers.
The second year, wuchen.
At twenty-three I gave up the school that year and took up a school again at Gaozuo, because of the burden of the household.
The third year, jisi.
At twenty-four I was invited that year to a school at Jinshan, where I stayed a year.
The fourth year, gengwu.
At twenty-five I again accepted the invitation to the school at Jinshan that year.
The fifth year, xinwei.

At twenty-six, because of the fire at this monastery, I had resolved to restore it, and to practice in order to nourish the Way while awaiting the time. That year I wished to travel far, and first went with Brother Xuelang En to roam Mount Lu. Reaching Nankang, I heard that the mountain was overrun with tigers and did not dare climb it, so I took a boat to Ji’an and visited Qingyuan, where I saw the monastery in ruins and the monks all wearing their hair long; moved, I resolved to restore it. I spoke to those in authority, and all under forty years of age were selected and shaved, more than forty men. In summer I returned from Qingyuan and set my own teacher’s affairs in order, arranging them well. In the eleventh month of winter I set out with a single bowl to travel far. When I was about to go north, Xuelang tried to stop me, fearing I could not endure the bitter cold, and urged me for the time being to go through Wu and Yue, where there are many fine mountains and rivers to delight the eye. I said, ‘Our habitual tendencies cling to comfort and warmth, and only in a place where they cannot be indulged are they easily subdued. Wu and Yue are but pillow and mat.’ So with a single bowl I set out on the long road.
